guides.title: Theories of Justice
guides.summary: A survey of how philosophers and jurists have answered the question of what a just society owes its members, from Plato and Aristotle through utilitarianism, Rawls, Nozick, Marx, the capability approach, and theories of global, criminal and ecological justice.

sections.heading: What Justice Is, and Why Competing Theories Exist
sections.body:
Justice is the virtue of institutions. Where honesty and courage are qualities of persons, justice is chiefly a property of the arrangements by which people live together: who gets what, who decides, who is punished and on what grounds, and who counts as a member entitled to be considered at all. Almost everyone agrees that justice matters and that it means treating people as they deserve to be treated. Disagreement begins the moment anyone asks what people deserve, and that disagreement is not a failure of clear thinking. It reflects the fact that justice sits at the intersection of several values that genuinely pull in different directions.

Consider a concrete case. A hospital has one liver and four candidates: a fifty-year-old surgeon with two children, a nineteen-year-old with a congenital defect, a sixty-eight-year-old who has waited longest, and a forty-year-old whose liver failed from alcohol dependence. Every plausible allocation rule picks a different winner. Maximising life-years saved favours the nineteen-year-old. Maximising social contribution favours the surgeon. First come, first served favours the sixty-eight-year-old. Equal chance regardless of history favours a lottery among all four. Holding people responsible for their choices disfavours the fourth. Each rule expresses a real conception of justice, and no purely factual investigation settles which is right.

This is why theories of justice exist. A theory is an attempt to give a systematic and defensible account of which considerations count, how they are weighted, and what follows for the design of institutions. A good theory does three things. It organises intuitions, showing that a scattered set of judgments about taxation, punishment, inheritance and healthcare rest on a smaller set of underlying commitments. It generates verdicts in new cases where intuition is silent or divided, such as the distribution of vaccines during a pandemic or the ownership of data. And it exposes inconsistency, forcing a person who wants both strict property rights and a generous welfare floor to say how the two fit together.

A useful early distinction is between the concept of justice and conceptions of it. H. L. A. Hart drew this line in The Concept of Law in 1961. The concept is thin and near-universally shared: treat like cases alike and different cases differently in proportion to their difference. Nobody disputes it, and it decides nothing on its own, because everything turns on which differences are relevant. Skin colour was long treated as relevant to the distribution of the franchise; almost nobody now defends that. Effort, need, contribution, prior agreement and sheer chance are all live candidates. A conception of justice is a filled-in answer specifying which differences matter and why. Nearly every real political argument, including those conducted in the language of rights or fairness, is a dispute between conceptions rather than about the concept.

sections.heading: Ancient Foundations: Plato, Aristotle and Giving Each Their Due
sections.body:
Systematic thinking about justice in the Western tradition begins with Plato's Republic, written around 380 BCE. The dialogue opens with three ordinary definitions and demolishes each. Cephalus proposes that justice is telling the truth and paying debts; Socrates replies that returning a borrowed weapon to a friend who has since gone mad would be unjust. Polemarchus proposes helping friends and harming enemies; Socrates replies that harming anyone makes them worse, and it cannot be the work of justice to produce injustice. Thrasymachus proposes, with real force, that justice is simply the advantage of the stronger, a set of rules the powerful impose and call moral. Answering Thrasymachus occupies the rest of the work, and the challenge he raises, that justice is a mask for power, recurs in Marx, Nietzsche, Foucault and modern critical theory.

Plato's own answer is structural. A city is just when each of its three classes, the producers, the guardians and the rulers, does its own proper work and does not meddle in the work of the others. The soul mirrors the city, with appetite, spirit and reason standing in the same relation, and a person is just when reason rules. Justice therefore is a kind of internal harmony rather than a rule of distribution. The account is famously demanding and famously illiberal: the ideal city features censorship, eugenic breeding and rule by philosopher-kings selected by a rigorous forty-year education. Karl Popper attacked it in 1945 as the fountainhead of totalitarian thinking, an accusation still argued over.

Aristotle, in Book V of the Nicomachean Ethics, produced the analytic framework that most later work still uses. He separated general justice, meaning lawfulness and complete virtue toward others, from particular justice, which concerns fairness in distributions and transactions. Particular justice he then divided in two. Distributive justice governs the allocation of honours, offices and goods, and follows a geometric proportion: shares should be in proportion to merit, so that if A deserves twice what B deserves, A's share should be twice B's. Corrective justice governs transactions and wrongs, and follows an arithmetic proportion, restoring the parties to equality by taking the gain from the wrongdoer and returning the loss to the victim, without regard to the merit of either party.

Aristotle also saw the deep problem clearly. Everyone agrees distribution should track merit, but democrats say merit is free birth, oligarchs say wealth, and aristocrats say virtue. The disagreement is about the currency of desert, not about the formula. The Roman jurist Ulpian later compressed the whole tradition into a formula that entered the Digest of Justinian in 533 CE: justice is the constant and perpetual will to render to each his due, suum cuique tribuere. It remains the most quoted definition in the history of law, and it is entirely empty until someone specifies what is due.

sections.heading: The Four Domains: Distributive, Corrective, Procedural and Retributive
sections.body:
Arguments about justice go wrong most often because the parties are discussing different domains without noticing. It pays to separate four, each with its own logic, its own characteristic institutions and its own standards of success.

Distributive justice concerns how benefits and burdens are shared across a society: income, wealth, healthcare, education, political power, exposure to pollution, liability for taxes and military service. Its questions are what the currency of distribution should be, what pattern is required, and who is included in the pool. Competing principles include strict equality, distribution according to need, according to contribution, according to effort, and according to whatever emerges from voluntary exchange. Real tax and welfare systems are compromises among several of these, which is why they rarely satisfy anyone completely.

Corrective justice, sometimes called rectificatory or commutative justice, concerns the repair of wrongful losses between particular parties. It is the domain of contract, tort and restitution. Its logic is strictly bilateral: the question is what this defendant owes this claimant because of what passed between them, and the defendant's overall wealth or virtue is formally irrelevant. Ernest Weinrib has argued influentially since the 1990s that this bilateral structure is what makes private law intelligible as something other than disguised regulation, and that attempts to justify tort law by its deterrent effects misdescribe what courts actually do.

Procedural justice concerns the fairness of the process rather than the outcome. John Rawls drew a threefold distinction that has proved durable. Perfect procedural justice exists where there is an independent criterion of a fair outcome and a procedure guaranteed to produce it, as with the cake-cutting rule that one child divides and the other chooses. Imperfect procedural justice exists where there is an independent criterion but no procedure guaranteed to reach it, as with criminal trials, which aim at convicting the guilty and acquitting the innocent yet sometimes fail. Pure procedural justice exists where there is no independent criterion at all and the outcome is fair simply because the procedure was, as with a fairly conducted lottery. Empirical work by Tom Tyler from the 1980s onward shows that people's willingness to accept adverse outcomes and to comply with law depends heavily on whether they judged the process fair, often more than on the outcome itself.

Retributive justice concerns the state's response to wrongdoing: whether to punish, how much, and on what grounds. Its central questions are what justifies imposing suffering deliberately, and what proportion means when converting a wrong into months of imprisonment. Restorative justice is a rival within this domain, treating crime primarily as harm to relationships to be repaired through dialogue and reparation rather than as a debt paid in punishment.

A rule can satisfy one domain and violate another. Bankruptcy discharge is often defended distributively as preventing lifelong destitution, and criticised correctively as denying creditors what they are owed. Naming the domain in dispute usually clarifies more than any further argument within it.

sections.heading: Natural Law, Natural Rights and the Social Contract
sections.body:
A second great tradition asks not what pattern a distribution should follow but by what authority anyone is bound at all. Its answer is that political obligation rests on a foundation prior to any particular state: either a moral order discoverable by reason, or an agreement that rational people would make.

Natural law is the older strand. Cicero wrote in De Re Publica around 51 BCE that true law is right reason in agreement with nature, unchanging and eternal, and that no senate can absolve us from its obligation. Thomas Aquinas gave the systematic Christian version in the Summa Theologiae in the 1270s, distinguishing eternal law, natural law accessible to human reason, divine law revealed in scripture, and human positive law. His most consequential claim is that an unjust human law is a corruption of law rather than law properly so called, lex iniusta non est lex. That formula supplied the language of resistance for centuries and was invoked directly by Martin Luther King in the Letter from Birmingham Jail in 1963, and by the prosecutors at Nuremberg in 1945 against the defence that officials had merely followed the law of their state.

Social contract theory reframes the question in secular terms by asking what people would agree to. Thomas Hobbes, writing in Leviathan in 1651 with the English Civil War fresh in memory, began from a state of nature in which there is no common power, no industry, no arts, and life is solitary, poor, nasty, brutish and short. Rational self-interest alone drives people to transfer their rights to a sovereign whose authority must be near absolute, because any right of resistance would reopen the door to civil war. Justice for Hobbes has no existence before the covenant: where there is no common power there is no law, and where there is no law there is no injustice.

John Locke, in the Second Treatise of Government of 1689, rejected the bleakness of the premise and the absolutism of the conclusion. His state of nature already contains a law of nature binding on all, granting rights to life, liberty and estate. Government is instituted by consent for the limited purpose of protecting those rights, holds power in trust, and forfeits legitimacy if it violates them, which grounds a right of revolution. Locke also offered the most influential account of how private property arises without consent: mixing one's labour with unowned nature makes the product one's own, subject to the proviso that enough and as good is left for others. That proviso has been fought over ever since, because in a finished world nothing is left unowned.

Jean-Jacques Rousseau, in The Social Contract of 1762, shifted the emphasis from protection to freedom, arguing that legitimate authority requires each person to obey only the general will, which is the will aimed at the common good rather than the sum of private interests. The formula is inspiring and dangerously elastic, since it permits the claim that a dissenter is being forced to be free, and critics from Benjamin Constant onward have said so.

sections.heading: Kant, Dignity and Justice as Respect for Persons
sections.body:
Immanuel Kant supplied the moral foundation on which most contemporary rights-based theories of justice are built, and did so without appealing to God, to consequences or to actual agreement. His starting point is that a rational being has a distinctive standing: things have a price and can be exchanged for equivalents, but persons have dignity, which admits of no equivalent. From this he derives the formula of humanity, stated in the Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals of 1785: act so that you treat humanity, whether in your own person or that of another, always as an end and never merely as a means.

The word merely does considerable work and is frequently misread. Kant is not forbidding the use of other people. Hiring a plumber uses the plumber as a means to a repaired pipe, and there is nothing wrong with that, because the plumber has agreed on terms they could rationally accept and retains their own ends. What is forbidden is treating a person purely as an instrument, in a way they could not possibly consent to as a rational agent: deceiving them, coercing them, or disposing of them for someone else's benefit. This is why Kantian theories are so resistant to the sacrifice of individuals for aggregate gain, and why they underwrite the modern law of informed consent in medicine and research, formalised after Nuremberg in 1947 and refined in the Declaration of Helsinki from 1964.

Kant's political philosophy, set out in the Metaphysics of Morals of 1797, makes right, Recht, the whole set of conditions under which the freedom of each can coexist with the freedom of everyone else under a universal law. Justice therefore is not about happiness or welfare at all but about compatible spheres of external freedom. This yields a strong duty to leave the state of nature and enter a civil condition, since without public authority nobody's rights are more than provisional; it yields a republican constitution with separated powers; and it grounds the innate right to freedom that every person possesses simply as a person, independent of any legal system.

On punishment Kant was severe. He rejected deterrence as a justification because it uses the offender as a mere means to the safety of others, and insisted that punishment be imposed only because the offender has committed a crime, in a measure equal to the wrong. His notorious illustration is that if a civil society were to dissolve by common agreement, the last murderer in prison must first be executed, so that everyone realises the desert of their deeds. Few modern Kantians follow him that far, but the underlying structure, that punishment must be deserved and proportionate rather than merely useful, remains the strongest available argument against punishing an innocent person to prevent a riot.

The standing difficulty is Kant's formalism. The theory tells you to respect persons and to universalise your maxim; it says relatively little about how to weigh competing claims when two people's freedoms genuinely conflict, which is most hard cases.

sections.heading: Utilitarianism: Justice as Aggregate Welfare
sections.body:
The most powerful modern rival to rights-based thinking holds that institutions should be judged by their consequences for well-being, and that a just arrangement is simply the one producing the greatest sum of good. Jeremy Bentham gave the doctrine its slogan and its method in An Introduction to the Principles of Morals and Legislation of 1789: the greatest happiness of the greatest number is the measure of right and wrong. He dismissed the natural rights of the French declaration as nonsense upon stilts, and imprescriptible natural rights as nonsense upon stilts, because a right for Bentham is a creature of law and nothing else.

The attractions are real and should not be underrated. Utilitarianism is impartial in a radical way, counting each person for one and nobody for more than one, which made it a solvent of aristocratic privilege. Bentham applied it to argue for prison reform, animal welfare on the ground that the question is not whether animals can reason but whether they can suffer, and the decriminalisation of homosexuality in an essay written around 1785 that was too dangerous to publish. It gives a clear decision procedure where rights talk often stalls, and it is the working framework of cost-benefit analysis, of public health prioritisation and of the quality-adjusted life year used by bodies such as the United Kingdom's National Institute for Health and Care Excellence, which has historically treated interventions costing roughly twenty to thirty thousand pounds per QALY as cost-effective.

John Stuart Mill refined the doctrine in Utilitarianism of 1861 by insisting that pleasures differ in quality as well as quantity, famously preferring to be Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied. More importantly for justice, Mill argued in the fifth chapter that our strong feelings about justice are not an exception to utility but a recognition of the most vital class of utilities: rules protecting security are so fundamental to every other good that we sensibly treat them as near-absolute. This produced the tradition of rule utilitarianism, which evaluates rules rather than individual acts, and which grounds rights as unusually well-justified rules.

The standing objection is that maximising a sum permits sacrificing individuals. If framing an innocent person would quell a riot and save five lives, straightforward act utilitarianism appears to require it. If a small minority can be made to suffer greatly for a large diffuse benefit, the arithmetic can approve. Utilitarians reply that in practice such policies corrode trust and produce worse outcomes, which is often true but is an empirical bet rather than a principled barrier. John Rawls put the deepest version of the objection in 1971: utilitarianism does not take seriously the distinction between persons, because it extends to society as a whole the principle of rational choice for one person, treating gains for some as straightforwardly compensating losses for others, when in fact there is no single subject who experiences both.

sections.heading: Rawls: The Original Position and Justice as Fairness
sections.body:
John Rawls's A Theory of Justice, published in 1971, revived political philosophy as a serious academic discipline almost single-handedly and remains the work every subsequent theory has had to answer. Its ambition was to produce a systematic alternative to utilitarianism that could match its rigour while refusing to sacrifice individuals to aggregate gain.

Rawls's method is a device of representation he calls the original position. Imagine parties choosing the basic principles that will govern the fundamental institutions of their society, its constitution, its economy, its property rules. They are rational and self-interested, wanting as large a share as possible of what he calls primary goods: rights and liberties, opportunities, income and wealth, and the social bases of self-respect. But they choose behind a veil of ignorance. They do not know their own class, race, sex, natural talents, state of health, religious convictions or conception of the good life. They do not know which generation they belong to. They know general facts about economics, psychology and society, but nothing that identifies them personally.

The veil is the engine of the whole theory, and its point is to model fairness by construction. Bias requires knowing which way to be biased. A person who does not know whether they will be rich or poor, able-bodied or disabled, of the majority religion or a persecuted minority, cannot rig the rules in their own favour, and so is forced to consider the position of everyone. Rawls calls the result justice as fairness: principles are just because they emerge from a procedure that is fair, an instance of pure procedural justice.

Rawls argues that parties so situated would reason conservatively, following something like a maximin rule: when the stakes are the whole shape of your life, when you cannot assign meaningful probabilities to landing in any particular position, and when some outcomes are intolerable, choose the option whose worst outcome is best. Gambling on being wealthy in a society with slavery is irrational when the downside is slavery and you cannot buy insurance afterwards.

The original position is not a historical claim and Rawls never suggested it was. It is a thought experiment for testing principles, closely related to the older test of asking whether you would accept a rule if you did not know which side of it you would be on, and to the cake-cutting rule where the divider takes the last slice. Rawls paired it with a second methodological idea, reflective equilibrium: we work back and forth between our principles and our considered judgments about particular cases, adjusting each until they cohere. If a principle implies that slavery could be just, we reject the principle; if a firmly held judgment cannot be systematised at all, we may revise the judgment.

Critics have pressed hard on whether the parties would really reason as Rawls says. John Harsanyi argued in 1975 that rational choosers behind the veil, assigning equal probability to each position, would maximise expected utility and thereby choose average utilitarianism instead. The dispute turns on whether risk aversion of the extreme kind Rawls assumes is rational, and it has never been decisively settled.

sections.heading: Rawls's Two Principles and the Difference Principle
sections.body:
The substance of Rawls's theory lies in the two principles he argues would be chosen behind the veil of ignorance, and in the strict priority ordering between them. The formulation matters, because a great deal of both praise and criticism has been aimed at misstatements of it.

The first principle is the liberty principle: each person has an equal claim to a fully adequate scheme of equal basic liberties, compatible with the same scheme for all. The basic liberties are enumerated rather than derived from an abstract idea of freedom, and include freedom of thought and conscience, freedom of association, political liberty including the right to vote and hold office, freedom of the person and from arbitrary arrest, and the right to hold personal property. Notably, freedom of contract and the right to own productive means are not on the list, which is why Rawls's theory is compatible with either a property-owning democracy or liberal socialism, but not with laissez-faire capitalism.

The second principle has two parts. Social and economic inequalities are to be arranged so that they are, first, attached to offices and positions open to all under conditions of fair equality of opportunity, and second, to the greatest benefit of the least advantaged members of society. That second clause is the famous difference principle.

The priority rules are as important as the principles. Liberty comes first and cannot be traded for economic gain: you may not sell the vote of a minority in exchange for prosperity, however large. Fair equality of opportunity comes before the difference principle: you may not compensate for a rigged competition by paying the losers. Rawls calls this lexical ordering, meaning you fully satisfy the first before considering the second, as with alphabetical ordering of words.

The difference principle is widely misunderstood as requiring equality. It does not. It permits, and may require, substantial inequality, provided the inequality actually improves the absolute position of the worst-off group. If paying surgeons four times the median wage produces better healthcare for the poorest, the inequality is justified. If it merely enriches surgeons without improving the floor, it is not. The test is comparative against feasible alternatives, not against a state of nature. Fair equality of opportunity is likewise stronger than formal non-discrimination: it requires that people with the same native talent and the same willingness to use it should have the same prospects regardless of the social class they were born into, which has demanding implications for inherited wealth and for the funding of schools.

Rawls later revised the framework substantially in Political Liberalism of 1993, conceding that his earlier presentation had treated justice as fairness as a comprehensive moral doctrine, and recasting it as a political conception that citizens holding deeply different religious and philosophical views could nonetheless endorse through an overlapping consensus. The change is not cosmetic; it reflects his judgment that reasonable pluralism about the good life is the permanent condition of a free society.

sections.heading: Nozick, Entitlement, and the Libertarian Challenge
sections.body:
Robert Nozick's Anarchy, State, and Utopia appeared in 1974, three years after Rawls and partly in response to him, and remains the sharpest statement of the view that justice concerns the history of holdings rather than their pattern. Nozick begins from a Lockean premise stated at maximum strength: individuals have rights, and there are things no person or group may do to them without violating those rights. Rights function as side constraints on action rather than as goals to be maximised, which means you may not violate one person's rights even to minimise total rights violations.

His entitlement theory of distributive justice has three parts. A holding is just if acquired justly from unowned nature, the principle of justice in acquisition. A holding is just if transferred voluntarily from someone who held it justly, the principle of justice in transfer. And where either principle was violated, a principle of rectification applies to correct past injustice. If a distribution arose through a chain of just acquisitions and voluntary transfers, it is just, however unequal it looks. There is no further test to apply.

Nozick's most effective argument against pattern-based theories is the Wilt Chamberlain example. Suppose a distribution D1 is perfectly just by whatever pattern you favour, including strict equality. A million people each voluntarily pay twenty-five cents extra to watch Chamberlain play basketball, and he ends the season with two hundred and fifty thousand dollars more than anyone else, producing D2. If D1 was just and every transfer was voluntary, how can D2 be unjust? The argument's force is that maintaining any pattern requires continuous interference with voluntary exchanges between consenting adults. Liberty, Nozick writes, upsets patterns.

He pushes further with the claim that taxation of earnings from labour is on a par with forced labour, since seizing the product of n hours of work is like forcing someone to work n hours for another's purposes. The provocation is deliberate and the analogy is imperfect, since taxpayers retain choice over occupation and hours, but it forces defenders of redistribution to say why the two cases differ.

Nozick's positive conclusion is the minimal state, limited to protection against force, theft and fraud and to the enforcement of contracts. He argues, ingeniously, that such a state could arise from anarchy by an invisible-hand process without violating anyone's rights, as dominant protective agencies emerge and compensate independents for prohibiting risky private enforcement.

The most serious objection is that his theory is hostage to its own principle of rectification. Actual holdings descend from conquest, slavery, expropriation and fraud on an enormous scale. Nozick admitted he had no worked-out theory of rectification, and speculated that in its absence something like a Rawlsian redistribution might be the best rough approximation. That concession is remarkable and is often overlooked by those who cite him. He also later described his own position as seriously inadequate in a 1989 book, though he did not abandon it.

sections.heading: Equality of What? Luck, Desert and Responsibility
sections.body:
Once you accept that a just society owes its members some form of equality, the immediate question is equality of what. Amartya Sen posed it under exactly that title in a 1979 lecture, and it has organised egalitarian theory ever since, because the candidate answers give radically different verdicts.

Equality of welfare says shares should be adjusted until people are equally satisfied. It has an obvious appeal and a fatal problem, identified by Ronald Dworkin in 1981: expensive tastes. A person who can only be content with plover's eggs and pre-phylloxera claret would be entitled to a far larger share than someone content with beer and sandwiches, which most people find perverse. Worse, it penalises the cheerful and rewards the sullen.

Equality of resources says shares of external goods should be equal, tested by Dworkin's imagined auction in which shipwreck survivors bid for the island's resources with equal clamshells until nobody envies another's bundle. This handles expensive tastes, since you pay for your own preferences, but it ignores unequal internal endowments: two people with identical resources fare very differently if one is blind. Dworkin's answer was a hypothetical insurance market in which people, ignorant of their own risk of disability, choose coverage, with the resulting premiums and payouts modelled by tax and transfer.

Behind these lies a deeper move that came to be called luck egalitarianism, associated with G. A. Cohen, Richard Arneson and Dworkin himself. Its principle is that inequalities traceable to brute luck, the circumstances nobody chose, are unjust and should be neutralised, whereas inequalities traceable to option luck, the outcomes of deliberate gambles, are acceptable. Born with a genetic illness is brute luck; losing money at roulette is option luck. The distinction has real intuitive traction and drives a great deal of ordinary reasoning about desert.

It also faces a powerful objection, pressed by Elizabeth Anderson in a 1999 paper titled What Is the Point of Equality? She argued that luck egalitarianism produces a demeaning politics in which citizens must present themselves as victims of misfortune to qualify for aid, that it abandons people who make imprudent choices to destitution, and that it misidentifies the aim of equality altogether. On her relational or democratic account, the point of equality is not to equalise a metric but to end oppression and to establish a society in which people stand in relations of equality to one another, neither dominating nor subordinated. Philip Pettit's republican theory makes a similar move, defining freedom as non-domination, the absence of anyone's capacity to interfere arbitrarily, rather than as non-interference.

The practical stakes are visible in welfare policy. Conditionality regimes, work requirements and sanctions are luck-egalitarian in spirit, tracking responsibility. Unconditional basic income is relational in spirit, refusing to sort the deserving from the undeserving because the sorting itself is degrading and administratively costly. Neither position follows from equality as such; both are conceptions of it, and the choice between them is where most contemporary welfare argument actually lives.

sections.heading: Marx, Exploitation and the Critique of the Justice Frame
sections.body:
Karl Marx's relation to theories of justice is genuinely paradoxical and worth stating carefully, because it is misrepresented in both directions. His writings are saturated with the language of theft, robbery and plunder, and yet he repeatedly denied that his critique of capitalism was a moral critique, and mocked talk of equal rights and fair distribution as ideological rubbish.

The analytical core is the theory of exploitation set out in Capital, volume one, published in 1867. Marx argues that labour power is a commodity with a peculiar property: its use produces more value than its own reproduction costs. A worker paid the equivalent of four hours of socially necessary labour may work an eight-hour day, and the surplus value of the remaining four hours is appropriated by the owner of the means of production. The transaction is voluntary in the legal sense and the worker receives the market value of what they sell. Exploitation on this account is therefore not cheating; it is a structural feature of a system in which one class owns productive assets and the other must sell its labour to live.

This is why Marx resisted the justice frame. In the Critique of the Gotha Programme of 1875 he attacked the German socialists for demanding a fair distribution of the proceeds of labour, asking what fair means and answering that every mode of production generates its own standard of justice: the capitalist wage bargain is just by capitalist standards, and denouncing it as unjust merely applies one historically produced standard to another. Distribution, he insisted, is a consequence of the relations of production, so a movement fixated on redistributing income while leaving ownership untouched has mistaken the symptom for the disease.

The same text gives his one concrete sketch of post-capitalist distribution, in two stages. In the first, immediately after capitalism, workers are paid according to labour contributed, a standard he calls an equal right that is still a bourgeois right, because it tacitly treats unequal individuals by an equal measure and ignores that one worker has more children or worse health. Only in a higher phase, after the springs of cooperative wealth flow more abundantly, can society inscribe on its banners: from each according to his ability, to each according to his needs.

Whether Marx had a theory of justice despite himself has been debated for fifty years. Allen Wood argued in 1972 that he genuinely did not and that capitalism is condemned for its effects on human flourishing, freedom and self-realisation rather than for injustice. G. A. Cohen replied that Marx thought capitalism unjust but did not think he thought so. Analytical Marxists including Cohen and John Roemer subsequently reconstructed exploitation without the labour theory of value, defining it instead in terms of unequal initial ownership of productive assets, which is a more defensible formulation and connects directly to luck egalitarianism.

sections.heading: Community, Virtue and Separate Spheres
sections.body:
Through the 1980s a family of critics argued that the liberal theories dominating the field had a false picture of the person and an impoverished picture of society. Loosely grouped as communitarians, though several rejected the label, they shared the view that justice cannot be derived from an abstract standpoint stripped of history, membership and shared meaning.

Michael Sandel's Liberalism and the Limits of Justice of 1982 aimed directly at Rawls's original position. The parties behind the veil, Sandel argued, are unencumbered selves: beings whose identity is prior to and independent of all their ends, attachments and commitments. But real people do not choose their family, their language, their nation or their inherited obligations; these are constitutive of who they are, not optional extras selected from a menu. A conception of justice built on a false anthropology, he argued, will systematically undervalue the goods of membership and mutual obligation.

Alasdair MacIntyre's After Virtue, also 1981, made a historical case. Modern moral argument, he claimed, is interminable because we are working with the fragments of older traditions whose contexts have been lost, using terms like rights and utility that once had meaning inside a shared account of human purpose and now function as expressions of preference dressed as reasoning. His remedy is a return to a virtue ethics grounded in practices, narrative identity and tradition, in which justice is a virtue exercised by persons inside a community with a shared conception of the good.

Michael Walzer's Spheres of Justice of 1983 offers the most usable version of the position. Walzer rejects the search for a single distributive principle covering all goods. Different social goods have different social meanings, and each meaning carries its own appropriate criterion: medical care should go by need, offices by qualification, punishment by desert, love by mutual affection, political power by persuasion. Injustice on his account is dominance, the conversion of advantage in one sphere into advantage in another where it does not belong. Money buying medical care beyond the basic level may be tolerable; money buying a court verdict, an election or an exemption from military service is what he calls a blocked exchange, and every society maintains a long list of things money must not buy. He calls the resulting ideal complex equality: not that everyone has the same, but that nobody's advantage in one sphere converts into general superiority.

The liberal reply is that these critiques often conflate a method with a metaphysics. Rawls insisted the veil is a device of representation for testing principles, not a claim that selves really are unencumbered. The sharper worry about communitarianism is conservative: if justice derives from shared meanings, a society whose shared meanings endorse caste or the subordination of women appears to be just by its own lights, and Walzer's own tools for internal criticism have struck many readers as too weak to do the work required.

sections.heading: The Capability Approach: Sen, Nussbaum and Real Freedom
sections.body:
Amartya Sen, an economist who won the Nobel Memorial Prize in 1998, developed an alternative that has had more practical influence on policy than any other contemporary theory of justice. Its starting question is what we should be measuring when we ask how well a person's life is going, and its answer rejects both income and subjective satisfaction.

Income is a poor measure because people differ enormously in their ability to convert resources into a life they value. A person with a disability may need two or three times the income of an otherwise identical person to achieve the same mobility. A pregnant woman has higher nutritional requirements than the household average implies. A person living in a society hostile to their religion may need more resources to achieve the same participation. Equal income can therefore mask deeply unequal real opportunity. Subjective satisfaction is a poor measure for the opposite reason, which Sen calls adaptive preference: people who have lived with deprivation adjust their expectations downward and report contentment. Surveys in India in the aftermath of the 1944 Bengal famine found widows reporting themselves in good health at rates similar to men, despite objectively worse conditions, because their standard of comparison had shifted.

Sen's proposal is to evaluate lives in terms of functionings, the various things a person may value doing or being, such as being adequately nourished, avoiding preventable disease, being able to move about, taking part in the life of the community, and appearing in public without shame. Capability is the set of functionings genuinely available to a person, the real freedom to choose among alternative lives. The distinction between fasting and starving captures the point exactly: the same functioning, being undernourished, but radically different capability sets, and it is the freedom that matters morally.

Martha Nussbaum extended the framework in a more definite direction by proposing a specific list of ten central capabilities that any decent society must secure to a threshold level: life; bodily health; bodily integrity; senses, imagination and thought; emotions; practical reason; affiliation; concern for other species; play; and control over one's political and material environment. She argues the list can be endorsed from many different moral and religious standpoints and should be written into constitutions as entitlements. Sen has consistently declined to endorse any fixed list, holding that the selection and weighting of capabilities is a matter for public reasoning and democratic deliberation in each context. That disagreement between them is real and unresolved.

The approach's practical footprint is large. The United Nations Human Development Index, introduced in 1990 and designed with Sen's involvement, combines life expectancy, education and income precisely to move measurement beyond gross domestic product. The Multidimensional Poverty Index, developed at Oxford from 2010, counts overlapping deprivations in health, education and living standards, and regularly identifies populations that income measures classify as non-poor. Sen's own most cited empirical claim, that no substantial famine has occurred in a functioning democracy with a free press, connects the framework directly to political capability.

sections.heading: Feminist Justice, Care and the Domestic Sphere
sections.body:
Feminist political philosophy has raised two distinct challenges to the mainstream tradition. The first concerns scope: the theories systematically ignored the family. The second concerns method: the model of the person and of moral reasoning is drawn from a narrow slice of human experience.

Susan Moller Okin's Justice, Gender, and the Family of 1989 made the scope objection decisively. She observed that the great theorists, Rawls included, treated the family as a private sphere outside the reach of principles of justice, or as the natural school of moral development, while never asking whether its internal distribution of labour, leisure, income and power was itself just. Yet the household is where the unequal division of unpaid work begins and where much of the lifetime inequality between men and women is generated. Time-use surveys across wealthy countries consistently find women performing between one and a half and two and a half times the unpaid domestic and care work of men, with the gap widening sharply after the birth of a first child. Okin argued that a theory taking fair equality of opportunity seriously cannot bracket this, and pressed the point that Rawls's own parties behind the veil, not knowing their sex, would not accept a gender-structured family. She noted that Rawls's occasional use of heads of households as the parties quietly assumed away the problem.

Carol Gilligan's In a Different Voice of 1982 launched the methodological challenge from developmental psychology. Studying responses to moral dilemmas, she argued that Lawrence Kohlberg's influential stage theory, which ranked abstract principled reasoning highest, systematically scored a different mode of reasoning as less mature: one focused on relationships, responsibility, context and avoiding harm to particular people rather than on adjudicating competing rights. Whether this pattern is reliably gendered has been contested and the empirical evidence is mixed at best, but the philosophical point survived independently of the psychology.

From it grew the ethics of care, developed by Nel Noddings, Virginia Held, Joan Tronto and Eva Feder Kittay. Its claims are that dependency is not an exceptional condition but the universal human one, since everyone begins helpless, many end so, and many live so throughout; that the liberal fiction of independent contracting adults is therefore a description of a temporary and privileged phase of life; and that care work, being socially necessary, should be recognised and distributed as a matter of justice rather than assumed as a natural female contribution. Kittay's work, informed by raising a daughter with severe cognitive disabilities, argues for a principle of doulia: just as we require care to survive, we owe support to those who care for others.

The relationship between care and justice remains disputed. Some theorists treat care as a rival to justice, some as a complement covering a domain justice cannot reach, and some, including Tronto, argue care is better understood as a political value requiring institutional provision rather than a private virtue.

sections.heading: Domination, Race and Historical Redress
sections.body:
A further body of work argues that mainstream theories of justice have been built on an idealisation that quietly writes out the actual history of the societies they describe, and that this omission is not incidental but distorting.

Charles Mills's The Racial Contract of 1997 makes the argument in the form of an inversion of social contract theory. The real contract underlying modern Western polities, he argues, was not among all persons but among those categorised as white, and it established a system in which non-whites were assigned subordinate status as a matter of political and legal structure rather than mere prejudice. On this reading the abstract egalitarian contract of Locke and Kant was written by theorists who simultaneously defended colonial appropriation, Locke having invested in the Royal African Company and drafted provisions for the Carolina colony, and Kant having published a racial hierarchy in his anthropological lectures. Mills's methodological complaint is against what he calls ideal theory: describing a well-ordered society that never existed, while treating the transition from actual injustice as a secondary problem, produces a philosophy that is useless precisely where it is most needed.

The practical question this raises is historical redress. If current distributions are downstream of expropriation, enslavement and exclusion, does justice require repair, and of what kind? The philosophical difficulties are real and should not be minimised. Identifying the wronged parties is hard when the direct victims are dead. Counterfactual reasoning about what descendants would have had is unstable, since different histories produce different people, a point Derek Parfit's non-identity problem sharpens uncomfortably. Determining who bears the cost is contested when much of the present population descends from later immigrants.

Counterarguments run in both directions. The forward-looking response, associated with Bernard Boxill and with Anderson's relational egalitarianism, sidesteps the counterfactuals by grounding the claim in present inequality that is demonstrably caused by past policy: in the United States, for instance, federally sanctioned mortgage redlining from 1934 and the exclusion of agricultural and domestic workers from the 1935 Social Security Act shaped a wealth gap that persists, with median white household wealth running roughly six to eight times median Black household wealth in recent surveys. On that framing, redress targets a live structural injustice rather than an ancestral debt.

Iris Marion Young's Justice and the Politics of Difference of 1990 offers a related structural account, arguing that the distributive paradigm itself is too narrow. Injustice, on her account, comprises five faces: exploitation, marginalisation, powerlessness, cultural imperialism and violence. Only the first is straightforwardly distributive; the others concern decision-making power, the division of labour and culture, and cannot be fixed by transferring goods. Her later model of political responsibility holds that agents connected to unjust structures share responsibility for reforming them without being individually blameworthy, a framework now widely used in debates about global supply chains.

sections.heading: Global Justice: Duties Beyond Borders
sections.body:
Almost every classical theory of justice assumes a bounded society, a single legal order with a common government. That assumption has become hard to defend. A person's life prospects are determined more by their country of birth than by any other single factor; the gap in life expectancy between the highest and lowest national averages exceeds thirty years; and roughly seven hundred million people live on less than the World Bank's extreme-poverty line, currently set at 2.15 international dollars per day in 2017 prices. Whether justice extends across borders is therefore among the most consequential live questions in the field.

Peter Singer opened the modern debate with a 1972 article written during the Bengal famine. His argument is short and hard to escape. If we can prevent something very bad from happening without sacrificing anything of comparable moral importance, we ought to do it. Distance and the presence of other potential helpers are morally irrelevant. Therefore affluent people are obliged to give until further giving would cost something of comparable importance, which is a far more demanding conclusion than conventional morality accepts. His shallow-pond illustration, that nobody would let a child drown to avoid ruining expensive shoes, is designed to show the intuition is already ours. The argument is best understood as a challenge: most people reject the conclusion while struggling to reject either premise.

Thomas Pogge shifted the ground from assistance to responsibility. In World Poverty and Human Rights of 2002 he argued that affluent countries are not merely failing to help but are actively imposing a global institutional order that foreseeably produces avoidable deprivation. He points to the international resource privilege, whereby whoever holds power in a country can sell its natural resources and confer valid title on buyers, and the international borrowing privilege, whereby they can contract debts binding on successors. Together these reward coups, entrench kleptocracy and inflict costs on populations who never consented. If that is right, the duty is negative, a duty not to harm, which is far easier to defend than an open-ended duty to rescue.

Against the cosmopolitans stand statists and liberal nationalists. Thomas Nagel argued in 2005 that egalitarian justice is associational: it arises only among people who are joint authors of coercively imposed institutions in whose name the coercion is exercised. Outside such a structure we owe humanitarian duties, which are real but weaker. David Miller defends national responsibility, arguing that special obligations among compatriots are legitimate and that peoples may be held responsible for their collective choices. Rawls himself, in The Law of Peoples of 1999, disappointed many admirers by declining to extend the difference principle globally, requiring instead only a duty of assistance to burdened societies until they can sustain decent institutions, and grounding differences in national wealth partly in domestic political culture.

The empirical premises matter and are contested. How much of cross-national inequality is attributable to global institutional structure rather than domestic governance is a genuinely open economic question, and one's answer largely determines which philosophical position looks plausible.

sections.heading: Intergenerational and Ecological Justice
sections.body:
Duties to people who do not yet exist strain every standard framework, because the usual machinery of justice assumes parties who can bargain, claim and reciprocate. Future generations can do none of these, and yet decisions made now about climate, nuclear waste, biodiversity and public debt determine the conditions of their lives more completely than almost anything they will decide for themselves.

Rawls addressed the problem with a just savings principle. Parties in the original position do not know which generation they belong to, so they must choose a rate of saving and investment they would accept whether they turned out to be early or late in the sequence. This yields a duty to maintain just institutions and to pass on the material base that sustains them, without requiring impoverishment of the present for an indefinitely richer future.

Derek Parfit exposed a much harder difficulty in Reasons and Persons in 1984, now called the non-identity problem. Consider two policies, depletion and conservation. Depletion produces a lower quality of life in two centuries, but it also changes who is conceived: different jobs, migrations and meetings mean entirely different individuals come to exist. The people living under depletion therefore cannot claim they were made worse off, since under conservation they would not have existed at all, and their lives are still worth living. Person-affecting morality, which holds that an act is wrong only if it wrongs some particular person, delivers the verdict that depletion harms nobody. Almost everyone finds that conclusion unacceptable, and no fully satisfying repair has been agreed. Parfit's own exploration of impersonal principles led him to the repugnant conclusion, that for any population with a high quality of life there is a much larger population with lives barely worth living that would be better, which he regarded as a reason to keep searching rather than a result to accept.

Economic practice sidesteps philosophy through the discount rate, and the choice is enormously consequential. The Stern Review of 2006 used a near-zero pure rate of time preference of 0.1 percent, on the ethical ground that future people's welfare counts equally, and concluded that aggressive early mitigation is worth roughly one to two percent of global output. William Nordhaus, using a market-calibrated rate near 3 percent, reached far more gradual conclusions. The disagreement is not primarily about climate science; it is about whether discounting future welfare is a defensible ethical position at all.

Ecological justice adds a further axis: whether non-human nature has standing in its own right, or only instrumentally through human interests. Christopher Stone's 1972 essay asking whether trees should have standing prompted real legal experiments, and several jurisdictions have since granted legal personhood to rivers, including the Whanganui in New Zealand in 2017 and the Ganges and Yamuna in an Indian court decision the same year. The practical function of such personhood is procedural, creating a guardian with standing to sue, and its long-term effectiveness remains uncertain.

sections.heading: Criminal Justice: Punishment, Deterrence and Restoration
sections.body:
Punishment is the hardest case for any theory of justice, because it requires justifying the deliberate infliction of suffering by the state on its own members. Three families of answer compete, and most real systems are unstable mixtures of all three.

Retributivism holds that punishment is justified because the offender deserves it. Wrongdoing creates a moral debt, and inflicting proportionate hard treatment is intrinsically right, not merely useful. Its great strengths are that it explains why we may not punish the innocent regardless of social benefit, and why the severity should track the seriousness of the offence rather than the difficulty of catching offenders. Its great weaknesses are that desert is hard to quantify and that the underlying intuition, that suffering can cancel wrongdoing, is difficult to defend without metaphor. Modern versions such as Antony Duff's communicative theory recast punishment as a form of censure addressed to the offender as a member of the moral community, aimed at repentance and reconciliation rather than at the balancing of a metaphysical ledger.

Consequentialist theories justify punishment by its effects: incapacitation, deterrence and rehabilitation. The empirical record is more mixed than public debate assumes. The best available evidence, surveyed repeatedly by Daniel Nagin and others, indicates that the certainty of apprehension deters substantially while the severity of sentences deters weakly or not at all, which is close to the opposite of how most sentencing policy is designed. Cesare Beccaria said as much in On Crimes and Punishments in 1764, arguing that it is the certainty of punishment, not its cruelty, that restrains. Incapacitation works while it lasts but has sharply diminishing returns as sentences lengthen past the age at which offending naturally declines, typically the mid-twenties. Rehabilitation programmes show real but modest effects, with well-designed cognitive-behavioural interventions reducing reoffending by perhaps ten to thirty percent relative to controls.

Restorative justice reframes the question entirely. Crime is treated as harm to people and relationships rather than as a violation of the state, and the response centres on a facilitated meeting among victim, offender and community to agree on repair. New Zealand made family group conferencing the default for youth offending in 1989. Meta-analyses generally find high victim satisfaction, running well above court processes, and modest reductions in reoffending. It works least well where power is grossly unequal, notably in domestic violence, where critics argue mediation risks re-victimisation.

Cutting across all three is a distributive question that theory long neglected: who is punished. Wrongful conviction rates, the effect of resources on outcomes, racial disparities in charging and sentencing, and the collateral consequences of a criminal record all mean a system may be defensible in its principles and grossly unjust in its operation. A retributivist who takes desert seriously has particular reason to care, since punishing beyond desert, or punishing those whose circumstances were themselves unjust, violates the theory on its own terms.

sections.heading: Reasoning Well About Justice: A Working Method
sections.body:
Theories of justice are not only for seminar rooms. Anyone drafting a policy, sitting on an allocation committee, designing a pay scale or arguing about a tax change is doing applied political philosophy, and doing it badly is expensive. A disciplined procedure will not tell you what is right, but it reliably improves the quality of the argument and exposes where the real disagreement lies.

The single most common error is arguing across domains without noticing. One party is making a corrective claim about what a particular person is owed; the other is making a distributive claim about the pattern across society; they talk past each other indefinitely. The second most common error is smuggling a contested premise into a definition, as when someone defines a tax as theft and treats the conclusion as established. The third is selective idealisation: applying strict market principles where they favour your side and appealing to need or desert where they do not.

A further habit is separating the principle from its application. Two people may agree that resources should follow need and disagree wholly about whether a particular applicant is needy, which is an empirical dispute masquerading as a moral one. Conversely, agreement about the facts with continuing disagreement about the verdict shows the dispute is genuinely about values, and should be conducted as such rather than by trading more statistics.
steps: Name the domain. Decide whether the question is distributive (who gets what across a group), corrective (what one party owes another for a wrong), procedural (whether the process was fair) or retributive (whether to punish). Different principles govern each.

State the currency. Say precisely what is being distributed or protected: money, real opportunity, capability, liberty, risk, standing. Arguments about equality are usually arguments about the currency.

Identify the pool. Say who is inside the scope of the principle and why. Citizens only, residents, future people, non-human animals, people abroad. Most heated disputes turn on an unstated answer here.
Write out the strongest version of the opposing principle, in terms its holders would accept. If your statement of it sounds absurd, you have not found it yet.
Apply the reversibility test. Would you accept this rule if you did not know which position in it you would occupy? If not, identify precisely which feature you are relying on.

Check the extremes. Push the principle to its limit and see what it licenses. One that permits sacrificing an innocent person, or forbids any redistribution to prevent starvation, sits at a boundary you must accept or explain away.

Separate the fact question from the value question. List which parts of the disagreement would be settled by better evidence and which would not. Pursue the first empirically; argue the second openly.

Ask what the rule does to relationships, not only to holdings. A transfer that relieves deprivation while requiring public self-abasement to qualify may fail on grounds a purely distributive test cannot see.

Decide, then record the residue. Note explicitly which competing claim you are overriding and at what cost. Justice rarely means all considerations point one way; honest practice means saying which one you sacrificed.

sections.heading: Failure Modes, Limits and Honest Uncertainty
sections.body:
Any survey of theories of justice should end by being candid about how much remains unsettled, because false confidence here does real damage. Two and a half thousand years of concentrated effort by very capable people has not produced convergence, and there are structural reasons to expect none.

The first limit is the plurality of values. Isaiah Berlin argued that genuine human goods conflict irreducibly: liberty and equality, mercy and desert, security and freedom, loyalty and impartiality. If he is right, there is no single scale on which trade-offs can be computed and no theory can be complete without loss. This is not relativism, since some arrangements are clearly worse than others on every scale, but it does mean the expectation of a decision procedure resolving every case is misplaced.

The second limit is the gap between theory and institution. A theory can be correct and unimplementable, because the institutions required to apply it would concentrate discretion in ways that invite abuse. Rules that are crude but predictable often outperform principles that are precise but require officials to make fine judgments about desert. This is the standard argument for formal equality before the law even where substantive justice would justify differentiation, and it is why administrability is a genuine moral consideration rather than a mere convenience.

The third is the ideal-theory problem raised by Sen, Mills and others. Specifying a perfectly just society may be neither necessary nor sufficient for identifying which of two feasible reforms is better. Knowing that Everest is the highest peak does not help you choose between two nearby hills. Most real decisions are comparative, and a theory built entirely around an ideal end-state may be silent exactly where guidance is needed.

The fourth is motivational. Even a correct theory does not deliver compliance. Institutions must be stable for the right reasons, in Rawls's phrase, meaning that people raised under them come to endorse them rather than merely submit. A conception of justice nobody can be brought to accept is a philosophical achievement and a political dead letter.

When an argument about justice stalls, three moves are usually productive. Retreat to cases: find a concrete example where you agree and work outward to locate where the paths diverge. Change the level: shift from principles to institutions, since people who disagree about foundations frequently agree about a specific reform, which is the overlapping consensus Rawls hoped for. And accept incompleteness: Sen's argument in The Idea of Justice of 2009 is that we can identify and remove manifest injustice, slavery, famine, torture, arbitrary imprisonment, without first agreeing on what perfect justice would look like. That is a considerably lower bar than the tradition set for itself, and there is a strong case that it is the bar that actually matters.

guides.title: Power, Authority & Legitimacy
guides.summary: How power is exercised, how it becomes authority, and what makes rule legitimate: the faces of power, Weber's types of authority, theories of consent and justification, the institutions that constrain rulers, and how legitimacy is built, measured, lost and rebuilt.

sections.heading: Three Concepts That Are Constantly Confused
sections.body:
Power, authority and legitimacy are distinct things that ordinary speech runs together, and almost every serious confusion about politics begins with that conflation. Power is the capacity to bring about outcomes despite resistance. Authority is the recognised right to issue binding commands. Legitimacy is the belief, held by those subject to rule, that the ruler's claim to that right is justified. A robber with a gun has power over you and no authority. A deposed monarch may retain a claim to authority with no power to enforce it. A government can hold both power and formal authority while enjoying almost no legitimacy — which is precisely the condition of a regime that must garrison its own capital.

The relationships between the three are causal but not automatic. Power without authority is exhausting: it must be applied continuously, at each point of contact, and it scales terribly. A state that can only compel through direct coercion has to place an enforcer beside every citizen, which is why totalitarian regimes are historically expensive and structurally fragile. Authority economises on power. When a police officer's instruction is obeyed because it is recognised as rightful rather than because a baton is visible, the same coercive capacity governs a hundred times as many people. Legitimacy, in turn, is what sustains authority over time and across generations. It is the reason tax compliance in most wealthy democracies runs above ninety percent while audit rates run around one percent — a ratio that is arithmetically impossible to explain by fear of detection alone.

This is the practical core of the subject: legitimacy is not decoration on top of power, it is the cheapest available substitute for it. The economist's version of the point is that enforcement costs rise steeply as voluntary compliance falls. The historian's version is that regimes rarely fall because an opposing army outguns them; they fall when the people who were supposed to hold the line stop believing the orders should be obeyed. In Eastern Europe in 1989, the coercive apparatus remained intact in every country that collapsed. What changed was the willingness of officials, conscripts and ordinary citizens to keep treating commands as binding.

The three concepts also come apart in ways that matter for judgement. Something can be legal without being legitimate — apartheid South Africa's pass laws were valid law, properly enacted, and widely regarded as void of moral force. Something can be legitimate without being legal, which is the standard defence of civil disobedience and of revolutionary constitutions, every one of which was illegal under the order it replaced. And something can be popular without being legitimate in the fuller sense, if the popularity is manufactured or if the majority is exercising power over a minority in ways that violate the terms on which authority was granted.

Getting these distinctions clear is the prerequisite for everything that follows, because the interesting questions in political life are almost always about the gaps between them.

sections.heading: Defining Power: From Dahl's Formula to the Three Faces
sections.body:
Robert Dahl offered the most-cited formulation in 1957: A has power over B to the extent that A can get B to do something that B would not otherwise do. The definition is deliberately behavioural and comparative. It implies that power is measurable in principle — you observe a decision, identify who prevailed against opposition, and attribute power accordingly. Dahl applied this in Who Governs?, his 1961 study of New Haven, Connecticut, examining decisions in urban redevelopment, education and party nominations, and concluded that different actors prevailed in different arenas. This supported pluralism: the view that power in a democracy is dispersed across competing groups rather than concentrated in a single elite.

Peter Bachrach and Morton Baratz replied in 1962 that this misses half the phenomenon. Their argument, the second face of power, is that the most effective exercise of power is keeping issues off the agenda entirely. If a factory owner's influence means that industrial pollution never reaches a council vote, an observer who studies only decisions will record no exercise of power at all. They called this non-decision-making, and it is empirically harder to study because it leaves an absence rather than a trace. The methodological move is to look for grievances that exist in the population but never surface as demands, and to ask what mechanism is filtering them out — procedural rules, the cost of organising, the reputation for retaliation, or the anticipated reaction that leads potential challengers to censor themselves.

Steven Lukes added a third face in Power: A Radical View in 1974. The most insidious power, he argued, shapes what people want in the first place. If B does what A wishes because B has come to believe it is in B's own interest, when a more accurate understanding would say otherwise, then A has exercised power without any conflict occurring at all. Lukes's example is that the supreme exercise of power is to prevent grievance from arising by shaping perceptions and preferences so that the existing order is accepted as natural, unchangeable or divinely ordained.

The third face is powerful analytically and genuinely problematic. It requires the analyst to distinguish a subject's expressed preferences from their real interests, which invites the criticism that the theorist is simply substituting their own judgement for the subject's and calling the disagreement false consciousness. Lukes acknowledged this in his 2005 second edition and softened the claim considerably. The honest position is that the third face identifies something real — advertising, national curricula, state media and religious instruction plainly shape preferences — while the inference from "B's preferences were shaped" to "B's preferences are not really B's" needs to be made case by case and defended, not assumed.

Michel Foucault pushed further still, arguing that power is not a possession held by actors but a relation woven through all social practice, producing knowledge, categories and subjects themselves. His account of disciplinary power — surveillance, examination, normalisation — describes mechanisms that operate in schools, clinics and workplaces without anyone commanding anything.

sections.heading: Weber's Three Pure Types of Legitimate Authority
sections.body:
Max Weber, writing in the first two decades of the twentieth century and published most fully in Economy and Society in 1922, produced the framework that still organises the field. He defined Herrschaft — usually translated as domination or authority — as the probability that a command will be obeyed by a given group. His question was why people obey, and he identified three pure types of claim to legitimacy, stressing that these are ideal types: analytic constructions that no real regime matches exactly, and which in practice appear in mixtures.

Traditional authority rests on the sanctity of immemorial custom. The ruler commands because that is how it has always been, and the appeal is to precedent rather than to reason or achievement. Hereditary monarchy, tribal chieftaincy, patriarchal household authority and gerontocracy are its forms. Weber distinguished patriarchalism, where the ruler governs through personal retainers with no separate administrative apparatus, from patrimonialism, where an administrative staff exists but is the ruler's personal instrument rather than an office-holding bureaucracy. The key structural feature is that there is no clear line between the ruler's private household and the public treasury, which is exactly why patrimonial systems and corruption are so hard to separate analytically.

Charismatic authority rests on devotion to the extraordinary personal qualities of an individual leader — the prophet, the war hero, the revolutionary founder. Weber took the term from theology, where charisma meant a gift of grace. The follower obeys not because of custom or rules but because of a perceived calling. Charismatic authority is inherently revolutionary because it appeals to no existing rule; the classic formula is "It is written, but I say unto you." It is also inherently unstable, because it depends on continued proof. A charismatic leader who suffers repeated defeat or fails to deliver promised transformation loses the basis of authority entirely. And it has no succession mechanism, which is the source of the most important process Weber described: the routinisation of charisma. When the founder dies, the movement must convert personal devotion into something transmissible — hereditary charisma, office charisma vested in a position, designation of a successor, or codification of the founder's teaching into rules. The history of most religions and most revolutionary states is a history of this conversion.

Legal-rational authority rests on belief in the legality of enacted rules and in the right of those elevated under them to issue commands. Obedience is owed to the impersonally ordered office, not to the person. Its characteristic administrative form is bureaucracy, which Weber described with a precision often mistaken for endorsement: hierarchy of offices, jurisdiction fixed by rules, written records, appointment on technical qualification, separation of office from officeholder, and a career with fixed salary and promotion. Weber considered this technically superior to all other forms, comparing it to machine production against non-mechanical methods, while also fearing it as an iron cage of rationalised, disenchanted existence.

sections.heading: Sources of Legitimacy: Consent, Performance, Legality, Identity
sections.body:
Weber's typology explains what claims rulers make. A separate question is what actually generates the belief that those claims are sound. Contemporary work generally identifies four families of legitimacy source, which operate simultaneously and can substitute for one another to a degree.

Consent-based legitimacy holds that authority derives from the agreement of the governed. This is the dominant modern claim and the foundation of social contract theory. Its operational form is competitive election: the ruler may command because a defined procedure, open to all, produced their selection. Consent theory's classic difficulty is that nobody actually consented to be born under a state. Locke's answer was tacit consent, inferred from continued residence and use of the highways; David Hume demolished this in 1748 by pointing out that a peasant who cannot speak the language and lacks the fare to leave is no more consenting than a sailor who did not jump overboard. Modern versions therefore rely less on historical consent and more on hypothetical consent — would rational people in fair conditions agree to these arrangements — which is the strategy John Rawls used in A Theory of Justice in 1971 with the original position and the veil of ignorance.

Performance legitimacy derives from delivering valued outcomes: security, order, economic growth, public health, functioning courts. This is sometimes called output legitimacy, in contrast to the input legitimacy of consent. Many regimes rest heavily on it. The People's Republic of China after 1978 is the standard example, where sustained growth averaging close to nine percent annually for three decades substituted for electoral authorisation. Performance legitimacy is powerful but brittle in a specific way: it is conditional on continued delivery, and it has no reserve. A regime legitimated by consent can survive a recession because the mandate was to govern, not to guarantee outcomes; a regime legitimated purely by performance faces an existential threat from the same recession.

Legal-procedural legitimacy derives from rules being followed. Even people who dislike an outcome will often accept it if the process was proper — the finding, well established in Tom Tyler's procedural justice research from the 1990s, that perceptions of fair process predict compliance and acceptance better than perceptions of favourable outcome. Tyler's studies of policing and courts identified four drivers: voice (the chance to be heard), neutrality, respectful treatment, and trustworthy motives.

Identity-based legitimacy derives from the ruler being one of us — sharing nationality, religion, ethnicity, class or historical experience with the ruled. It is the engine of nationalism and the reason imperial rule is so consistently unstable regardless of how well administered it is. British India was governed by an administratively competent civil service; the competence was irrelevant to the legitimacy problem. Identity legitimacy is potent, cheap and dangerous, because its logic implies that those outside the identity group have a weaker claim to the protections of the order.

sections.heading: The Social Contract Tradition and Its Critics
sections.body:
The idea that political authority originates in an agreement among the governed is the single most influential move in Western political thought, and it was made in three very different versions within a hundred and fifty years.

Thomas Hobbes published Leviathan in 1651, during the English Civil War, and his premise is a state of nature in which there is no common power. Because people are roughly equal in ability, because goods are scarce, and because anyone who does not strike first may be struck, life becomes a war of every man against every man — famously "solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short." Hobbes's argument is that rational individuals will therefore covenant with one another to transfer their rights to a sovereign, whose power must be absolute and undivided, since a divided sovereign is no sovereign and the alternative to absolute rule is a return to war. The only right retained is self-preservation: a condemned man may resist execution. Hobbes is the theorist of order as the primary political good, and his account remains the sharpest available statement of why even bad government beats no government.

John Locke's Second Treatise, published in 1689 in the aftermath of the Glorious Revolution, begins from a milder state of nature governed by natural law, where people hold rights to life, liberty and property, property arising from mixing one's labour with unowned resources. The problem is not war but the absence of an impartial judge. People therefore establish government as a trust for the limited purpose of protecting those pre-existing rights.
