The German regime signed a concordat with the Vatican in July 1933, then violated it systematically, promoted a nazified German Christian movement, harassed the dissenting Confessing Church of Martin Niemöller, who spent 1938 to 1945 in camps, and jailed thousands of clergy, while an inner circle nursed plans to settle accounts with Christianity after victory. Everyday life under fascism mixed coercion, inducement, and accommodation. Leisure was colonized by the dopolavoro and Strength Through Joy, which by 1938 had sent millions on subsidized excursions; consumption was politicized through campaigns for national products; denunciation became a social weapon, with Gestapo files showing that a large share of cases began with tips from neighbors, colleagues, and relatives, which let a police force of modest size, the Gestapo never exceeded about 32,000 officers for the whole Reich, surveil a nation of eighty million. Resistance existed on a spectrum from grumbling and nonconformity, like the swing youth who danced to forbidden jazz and the Edelweiss Pirates who brawled with the Hitler Youth, to the White Rose students Hans and Sophie Scholl, guillotined in February 1943 for leaflets, to the army officers around Claus von Stauffenberg whose bomb failed to kill Hitler on July 20, 1944, costing some 5,000 lives in reprisals.

sections.heading: Defeat, Justice, and Memory: 1945 and After
sections.body: Fascism as a regime form died in the rubble of 1945, and what followed set precedents that still govern international law and public memory. Mussolini was shot by Italian partisans on April 28, 1945; Hitler killed himself in his Berlin bunker two days later; Germany surrendered unconditionally on May 8. The victors then attempted something without precedent: judging a regime's leaders by law. The International Military Tribunal at Nuremberg, sitting from November 1945 to October 1946, tried 22 major figures for crimes against peace, war crimes, and a newly named category, crimes against humanity, convicting 19 and sentencing 12 to death; Göring cheated the gallows with cyanide. Twelve successor trials prosecuted doctors, judges, industrialists, and Einsatzgruppen commanders, and the Doctors' Trial produced the Nuremberg Code of 1947 on human experimentation, while the new word genocide, coined by the jurist Raphael Lemkin in 1944, entered law in the 1948 Genocide Convention, followed the same week by the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, both direct answers to fascism. Justice was nonetheless partial. Denazification in the western zones processed millions of questionnaires but collapsed into amnesties as the Cold War re-prioritized West German cooperation; by the mid-1950s most convicted perpetrators were free, and former party members re-entered civil service in large numbers. Italy's Togliatti amnesty of June 1946 released most fascist prisoners within a year, and no Italian Nuremberg ever examined colonial crimes in Libya and Ethiopia. Some perpetrators fled along ratlines to South America; Israeli agents captured Adolf Eichmann in Argentina in 1960, and his 1961 Jerusalem trial, which Hannah Arendt covered under the contested phrase the banality of evil, re-centered the Holocaust in world memory, as did later trials of Klaus Barbie in France in 1987 and camp guards into the 2010s, when German courts, reversing earlier doctrine, convicted men in their nineties as accessories for having served at death camps at all. Institutionally, the new democracies armored themselves. West Germany's Basic Law of 1949 created militant democracy: Article 21 allows the Federal Constitutional Court to ban anti-constitutional parties, used against the neo-Nazi SRP in 1952 and the Communist Party in 1956, and Article 1 makes human dignity inviolable and unamendable. Germany criminalized Holocaust denial and Nazi symbols under sections 86a and 130 of the criminal code; Austria's 1947 Verbotsgesetz did likewise; Italy's constitution bans refounding the Fascist Party, and the 1952 Scelba law criminalized apologia for fascism, though enforcement has been famously sporadic. The memory of fascism became a political institution in its own right: the German term Vergangenheitsbewältigung names the ongoing labor of working through the past, visible in school curricula, the Berlin Memorial to the Murdered Jews of Europe opened in 2005, and the stumbling-stone brass cobbles laid before deportees' homes across Europe, more than 100,000 of them by the 2020s. Italy's reckoning was shallower, cushioned by the postwar myth of the good Italian, italiani brava gente, which long obscured Italian war crimes in the Balkans and Africa and Italian complicity in deportations after 1943.

sections.heading: Neo-Fascism and the Postwar Radical Right
sections.body: Fascism survived 1945 as a political tradition, mutating to fit an environment in which the name itself had become toxic. In Italy, veterans of the Salò republic founded the Italian Social Movement, MSI, in 1946; it polled between 2 and 9 percent for four decades, kept the flame, fiamma tricolore, in its logo, and finally transformed itself in 1995, under Gianfranco Fini, into the post-fascist National Alliance, which formally renounced fascism, entered coalition governments, and eventually dissolved into the mainstream right, though successor symbolism and personnel persisted. West Germany's overtly neo-Nazi parties were contained by militant democracy, the SRP banned in 1952, the NPD peaking at 4.3 percent in 1969 and surviving two failed ban attempts in 2003 and 2017, while a violent underground persisted, most notoriously the National Socialist Underground cell exposed in 2011 after murdering ten people over a decade. Beyond parties, the tradition rebranded intellectually. The French Nouvelle Droite around Alain de Benoist from 1968 recast biological racism as ethnopluralism, the claim that cultures must be kept separate to be preserved, a formulation that migrated into twenty-first-century identitarian movements and the online alt-right, whose great replacement conspiracy theory, named by Renaud Camus in 2011, echoes interwar demographic panic and has been cited by mass shooters in Christchurch, El Paso, and elsewhere. Skinhead and terrorist currents, from Italy's Ordine Nuovo, implicated in the 1969 Piazza Fontana and 1980 Bologna station bombings, the latter killing 85, to the American neo-Nazi scene that produced The Turner Diaries in 1978 and inspired Timothy McVeigh's 1995 Oklahoma City bombing, kept the violent option alive. From the 1980s a broader radical right populism arose across democracies, the French National Front under Jean-Marie Le Pen, the Austrian Freedom Party, and many successors, parties that are anti-immigrant, nativist, and hostile to liberal institutions but compete in elections and disavow classical fascism. Political scientists, following Cas Mudde, generally class these as populist radical right rather than fascist, because they lack the palingenetic revolutionary project, the paramilitary seizure of power, and the totalitarian ambition, and the distinction is analytically important: calling every nativist party fascist obscures both what such parties actually are and what fascism actually was. The harder contemporary question is whether hybrid regimes and movements that hollow out democracy from within, through captured courts, media control, and permanent emergency, represent a functional successor even without the classical costume. Scholars such as Paxton insist the fascist label requires the mythic core and the violence; others, including Jason Stanley and the historian Timothy Snyder, argue that fascist technique, the politics of us and them, the leader who alone embodies the people, the assault on truth itself, travels freely without uniforms. Both camps agree on the empirical warning from the interwar years: fascism reached power nowhere by majority vote alone, and everywhere through the miscalculation of conservative elites who opened the door believing they could control what came through it. That lesson, unlike the black shirts, has never gone out of date.

sections.heading: Analytical Discipline: Using the Word Well and Reading the Signs
sections.body: The word fascism does real work only when used with discipline, and misuse has costs in both directions: promiscuous application numbs audiences and insults history's victims, while excessive fastidiousness can delay recognition until recognition is useless. A few rules of method help. First, compare against the whole syndrome, not a single trait. Militarism, censorship, nationalism, and leader worship each occur in many non-fascist systems; communist dictatorships shared several while resting on a different mythic core, class rather than nation, which is why most scholars treat them as a distinct totalitarian species. The fascist signature is the combination: palingenetic ultranationalism, a mass party glorifying violence, the leader fused with the people, enemies within marked for removal, and expansion abroad. Second, watch behavior over rhetoric, as Paxton urges: movements lie, and the diagnostic acts are the tolerated militia, the assault on independent courts and press, the criminalization of opposition, the treatment of political rivals as traitors rather than adversaries. Third, track stage, not just essence: a movement rooting itself in coalition with frightened conservatives is at a different and more dangerous point than a sect shouting on the margin, and the interwar record shows the decisive variable was rarely the fascists' strength alone but the establishment's choices, Victor Emmanuel declining martial law in 1922, Papen engineering the chancellorship in 1933. Fourth, respect base rates and context: economic crisis, humiliated nationalism, street violence normalized, and paralyzed parliaments formed the enabling weather; where institutions held, as in interwar Britain, Belgium, and the Scandinavian countries, and in the United States of the 1930s, kindred movements stalled. Historians also flag honest uncertainties that a careful reader should carry. The boundary cases, Franco, Salazar, imperial Japan, Vichy, remain genuinely contested, and the debate is substantive, not pedantic, because it turns on whether fascism requires a revolutionary project or merely brutal reaction. The relationship between fascism and modernity is likewise still argued: older views cast it as a revolt against modernity, while most current scholarship, following George Mosse and Griffin, sees it as an alternative modernism, embracing technology and mass society while rejecting liberal values. And the psychology of complicity, why ordinary people participate, remains an open research frontier running from Theodor Adorno's 1950 authoritarian personality studies through Stanley Milgram's 1961 obedience experiments to Browning's ordinary men, with the uncomfortable consensus that perpetrators are recruited from the normal population, not from monsters. For the citizen, the practical checklist is short. Democracies die today more often by increments than by marches on capitals: note when violence against opponents is excused as passion, when a leader claims to alone represent the true people while opponents become enemies of the nation, when courts, electoral machinery, and the press are captured rather than merely criticized, when a scapegoated minority is redefined out of the national community, and when a mythic lost greatness is promised through purification. None of these alone is fascism; their convergence is how it begins. The interwar generation lacked the concept and had to learn it at full price. Later generations own the concept, and with it the obligation to apply it accurately, neither everywhere nor nowhere.

guides.title: Green Politics & Political Environmentalism
guides.summary: The ideas, movements, parties, and policy tools of political environmentalism: where green politics came from, what it believes, how it wins and loses power, and how it shapes law from local ordinances to the global climate regime.

sections.heading: What Green Politics Is
sections.body: Green politics is the branch of political life that treats the relationship between human societies and the natural systems they depend on as a central question of government, rather than a technical detail to be managed after the important decisions are made. It is at once an ideology, a family of social movements, a set of political parties operating in more than ninety countries, and a body of policy practice ranging from municipal recycling ordinances to the Paris Agreement. What unifies these strands is a distinctive diagnosis: that industrial civilization has been drawing down its ecological capital, its stable climate, fertile soil, fresh water, forests, and biodiversity, faster than that capital regenerates, and that existing political institutions systematically undervalue the long term, the distant, and the nonhuman. From this diagnosis follow characteristic commitments. Greens argue that economic activity must operate within biophysical limits; that costs imposed on third parties through pollution, what economists call negative externalities, must be brought back onto the balance sheets of those who cause them; that future generations hold a moral claim on present decisions; and that environmental burdens must not be dumped on the poor and powerless, a concern known as environmental justice. Green politics is frequently misunderstood as single-issue nature protection, but from its formation in the 1970s it has been a broad program linking ecology with peace, social justice, and participatory democracy. It is also commonly misplaced on the conventional left-right spectrum. Green parties usually sit left of center on economics and social questions, yet the movement contains conservative conservationists, free-market environmentalists, religious stewardship traditions, and radical decentralists, and green thinkers have long insisted, in the slogan attributed to the early German Greens, that they are neither left nor right but in front. The stakes claimed by green politics are unusually concrete and measurable. Atmospheric carbon dioxide, about 280 parts per million before industrialization, passed 420 parts per million in the 2020s, and global mean surface temperature has risen roughly 1.2 to 1.3 degrees Celsius above the late nineteenth century baseline. The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, the United Nations body that synthesizes climate science, attributes essentially all of this warming to human activity. Beyond climate, the Living Planet Index reports steep average declines in monitored wildlife populations since 1970, and the concept of planetary boundaries, introduced by Johan Rockström and colleagues in 2009, argues that humanity has already crossed safe limits for climate, biodiversity loss, and nitrogen flows. Whether one accepts every green policy prescription or none, these numbers explain why environmentalism moved from the margins of politics to its center within two generations, why every major international institution now maintains an environmental agenda, and why understanding green politics, its history, its internal quarrels, its victories, and its persistent failures, has become necessary equipment for understanding modern government at every level.

sections.heading: Intellectual Roots: From Romanticism to Ecology
sections.body: Political environmentalism did not spring from nowhere in the 1960s; it braided together several older traditions. The first strand is romantic and literary. Reacting to the smoke and enclosure of early industrialization, writers such as William Wordsworth in England and Henry David Thoreau in America, whose Walden appeared in 1854, argued that wild nature carried moral and spiritual value that commerce could not price. John Muir carried this sensibility into activism, founding the Sierra Club in 1892 and campaigning, unsuccessfully, against the damming of Hetch Hetchy valley in Yosemite, an early template for environmental protest. The second strand is utilitarian conservation. Gifford Pinchot, first chief of the United States Forest Service under Theodore Roosevelt, promoted scientific management of forests for the greatest good of the greatest number for the longest time, a doctrine of sustained yield rather than preservation for its own sake. The tension between Muir's preservationism and Pinchot's conservationism, protect nature from use versus manage nature for use, still structures environmental debate today. The third strand is the science of ecology itself, a word coined by the German zoologist Ernst Haeckel in 1866, which matured in the twentieth century into a discipline showing quantitatively how energy and nutrients flow through interdependent living systems, and therefore how disturbance propagates. Aldo Leopold fused science and ethics in A Sand County Almanac, published in 1949, proposing a land ethic: a thing is right when it tends to preserve the integrity, stability, and beauty of the biotic community, and wrong when it tends otherwise. A fourth strand is the recurrent debate over population and resources, running from Thomas Malthus's 1798 essay on population through the twentieth-century arguments of Paul Ehrlich, whose 1968 book The Population Bomb forecast famines that largely did not arrive, teaching the movement a lasting lesson about the perils of overconfident prediction. Garrett Hardin's 1968 article The Tragedy of the Commons supplied a widely cited model of how unowned resources are overexploited, though the political scientist Elinor Ostrom later won the 2009 Nobel Memorial Prize in economics for documenting the many real communities that govern commons successfully without either privatization or central control, a finding greens invoke in favor of local, participatory management. Finally, there are non-Western and indigenous roots that the organized movement was slow to credit: traditions of reciprocity with land among Native American, Aboriginal Australian, Andean, and many African and Asian cultures, and movements such as the Bishnoi of Rajasthan, who protected trees and wildlife on religious principle centuries before the word ecology existed. Modern green politics inherited all of these: the romantic sense of nature's intrinsic worth, the conservationist's management tools, the ecologist's systems thinking, the Malthusian anxiety about limits, and a contested, still-unfinished reckoning with whose environmental knowledge counts.

sections.heading: The Awakening of the 1960s and 1970s
sections.body: The modern environmental movement has an unusually precise founding text: Silent Spring, published by the marine biologist Rachel Carson in September 1962. Carson documented how persistent pesticides, above all DDT, accumulated up food chains, thinned the eggshells of birds of prey, and threatened a spring without birdsong. The chemical industry attacked her fiercely, but President Kennedy's Science Advisory Committee vindicated her findings in 1963, and the United States banned most uses of DDT in 1972. Carson's deeper contribution was rhetorical: she taught a mass public to see pollution not as isolated nuisance but as systemic contamination of the web of life. The decade that followed supplied a drumbeat of confirming shocks. In 1969 an oil platform blowout coated the beaches of Santa Barbara, California, and Cleveland's chemically saturated Cuyahoga River caught fire, an event Time magazine made nationally famous. The Apollo missions returned photographs, Earthrise in 1968 and the Blue Marble in 1972, that showed the planet as a small, finite, borderless whole, images historians credit with crystallizing ecological consciousness. On 22 April 1970 Senator Gaylord Nelson's teach-in idea became the first Earth Day, drawing an estimated twenty million Americans, roughly a tenth of the country's population, into marches and teach-ins, still among the largest single-day demonstrations in American history. Political institutions responded with remarkable speed. The United States created the Environmental Protection Agency in December 1970 and passed the Clean Air Act of 1970, the Clean Water Act of 1972, and the Endangered Species Act of 1973, all with large bipartisan majorities, a fact worth remembering now that environmental law is sharply polarized. The National Environmental Policy Act of 1969 invented the environmental impact statement, a procedural device forcing agencies to analyze consequences before acting, which spread worldwide and remains one of environmentalism's most exported legal technologies. In 1972 the United Nations held its first environment conference in Stockholm, creating the United Nations Environment Programme, and a team at MIT led by Donella and Dennis Meadows published The Limits to Growth, a computer-model study commissioned by the Club of Rome which sold over ten million copies and argued that exponential growth in population and industrial output would overshoot planetary capacity within a century under business as usual. Its critics accused it of neo-Malthusian alarmism; its defenders note that the standard-run scenario has tracked subsequent data uncomfortably well. The 1973 OPEC oil embargo, quadrupling oil prices, added energy scarcity to the agenda and pushed governments toward both nuclear power and efficiency, splitting environmental opinion in ways that persist. By mid-decade the essential repertoire of modern environmental politics existed: popular science bestsellers, mass demonstrations, dedicated bureaucracies, framework statutes, impact assessment, international conferences, and a running argument about growth itself. What did not yet exist was a political party built on these ideas; that came next.

sections.heading: The Four Pillars and Core Green Values
sections.body: When greens organized into parties they needed a platform broader than pollution control, and the formula that traveled the world came from the founding program of the German Greens in 1980: four pillars supporting one politics. The first pillar is ecological wisdom, or Ökologie: human societies must live within the regenerative and absorptive capacities of ecosystems, taking the long view that markets and election cycles neglect. The second is social justice: environmental burdens and benefits must be fairly shared, and ecological policy that impoverishes the vulnerable is self-defeating, because insecure people cannot afford long horizons. The third is grassroots, or participatory, democracy: decisions should be made at the lowest effective level, by the people affected, through transparent institutions, decentralized power, and strong civil liberties. The fourth is nonviolence, extending from opposition to war and the nuclear arms race to a general preference for peaceful, lawful methods of social change. Later charters, such as that of the United States Green Party, expanded the four into ten key values, adding decentralization, community-based economics, feminism and gender equity, respect for diversity, personal and global responsibility, and future focus, and the Global Greens Charter adopted in Canberra in 2001 by parties from seventy-two countries consolidated six principles: ecological wisdom, social justice, participatory democracy, nonviolence, sustainability, and respect for diversity. Beneath the lists sit a few load-bearing concepts. The precautionary principle holds that when an activity risks serious or irreversible harm, scientific uncertainty is not a license to proceed; the burden of proof lies with the actor, not the potential victims. Sustainability, canonically defined by the 1987 Brundtland Commission as development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs, supplies the intergenerational test. Intrinsic-value arguments, associated with the deep ecology of the Norwegian philosopher Arne Naess, insist that other species matter for their own sake and not merely as resources, which is why green programs defend biodiversity even where no human use is at stake. Finally, greens are distinctive in questioning growth itself: where mainstream parties treat rising gross domestic product as the master indicator of success, greens argue that GDP counts the depletion of forests and aquifers as income and the costs of cleaning up disasters as production, and they promote alternative measures such as the Genuine Progress Indicator or wellbeing budgets of the kind New Zealand introduced in 2019. The four-pillar synthesis explains both green politics' breadth and its internal tensions. Ecology can collide with jobs, participation can slow urgent action, and nonviolence is tested by confrontational protest. But the pillars were a deliberate answer to a real question, whether ecology belonged to the left or the right, and their answer, that a livable planet requires justice, democracy, and peace together, remains the movement's common creed.

sections.heading: The First Green Parties
sections.body: The world's first green party at national level appeared not in Europe but in New Zealand: the Values Party, founded at Victoria University of Wellington in May 1972, contested that year's general election on a platform of zero economic growth, zero population growth, and quality of life, winning two percent of the vote, enough to introduce the template of a post-materialist party even though the first-past-the-post electoral system denied it seats. In Europe the pioneer was the United Kingdom's PEOPLE Party, founded in Coventry in 1973, which renamed itself the Ecology Party and eventually the Green Party; Switzerland elected the first green national parliamentarian, Daniel Brélaz, in 1979, and Belgium's Ecolo and Agalev won the first sustained parliamentary representation in 1981. The breakthrough that made green a global political brand came in West Germany. Die Grünen, founded in January 1980 in Karlsruhe, fused three currents: the anti-nuclear-power citizens' initiatives that had fought reactor sites like Wyhl in the 1970s, the peace movement opposing the stationing of NATO intermediate-range nuclear missiles under the 1979 twin-track decision, and the post-1968 new left alongside a smaller conservative conservation wing. Petra Kelly, a charismatic campaigner who had worked in the European Commission, became its best-known face. In the federal election of March 1983 the Greens crossed the five percent threshold with 5.6 percent and entered the Bundestag with twenty-seven seats, television images of sweaters and sunflowers among the dark suits announcing that something new had arrived in parliamentary politics. The young party institutionalized its distrust of power with rules that became famous: gender-balanced lists and dual male-female leadership, salary caps pegging parliamentarians' pay toward skilled-worker levels, and rotation, requiring deputies to surrender their seats mid-term to successors, a rule that proved unworkable and was abandoned by the late 1980s. Chernobyl's fallout over Europe in April 1986 validated the party's core warning and pushed environmental ministries into existence across the continent. Green parties multiplied through the 1980s, in Sweden, Austria, Finland, France, Italy, and beyond, and coordinated first through the European Greens federation founded in 1984, later the European Green Party of 2004, and globally through the Global Greens network established at Canberra in 2001. The early parties everywhere faced the same strategic dilemma, crystallized in the German quarrel between Fundis, fundamentalists who saw parliament as a tribune and coalition as corruption, and Realos, realists prepared to govern and compromise. The Realos won nearly everywhere, a victory sealed when Joschka Fischer, sworn in as Hesse's environment minister in 1985 wearing white trainers, went on to become German foreign minister and vice-chancellor in the 1998 red-green federal coalition. The trainers are now in a museum, which is roughly the movement's institutional biography in a single object.

sections.heading: Green Parties in Power and the Realo-Fundi Dilemma
sections.body: Once green parties began winning seats, the question became what to do with them, and Germany again supplied the laboratory. The red-green coalition of Social Democrats and Greens under Chancellor Gerhard Schröder governed from 1998 to 2005 with Joschka Fischer as foreign minister, and its record displays both faces of green government. On the achievement side stand the 2000 Renewable Energy Sources Act, whose feed-in tariffs guaranteed twenty-year above-market prices for solar and wind power and are widely credited with driving down the global cost of photovoltaics by creating mass demand; the 2002 nuclear phase-out agreement; an ecological tax reform shifting some taxation from labor onto energy; and a modernized citizenship law. On the compromise side, the party of pacifists voted in 1999 to send German aircraft into NATO's Kosovo campaign, the first German combat deployment since 1945, after Fischer told a raging party congress, punctuated by a thrown paint bag, that he had learned not only never again war but never again Auschwitz. Thousands of members resigned; the party governed on. The episode is the canonical illustration of the Realo-Fundi dilemma: office converts principles into policy only by converting some principles into casualties. Subsequent experience across Europe filled out the pattern. Greens have governed in coalition in Finland, first entering cabinet in 1995, Sweden, France, Belgium, Ireland, Austria, and elsewhere, usually as a junior partner trading votes on the broad program for control of environment, energy, and transport portfolios. Ireland's Greens were nearly annihilated in 2011 after sharing power through the financial crisis, then rebuilt and returned to government in 2020, a cycle, junior-partner blame absorption followed by slow recovery, so common it functions as a law of coalition politics. In Baden-Württemberg, Winfried Kretschmann became in 2011 the first green head of a German state government, repeatedly re-elected on a consciously conservative, business-friendly green platform, proving the brand could win beyond the urban left. The German Greens returned to federal office in the 2021 traffic-light coalition, holding the foreign ministry under Annalena Baerbock and an economy and climate super-ministry under Robert Habeck, and promptly met the hardest test yet: Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine forced green ministers to commission liquefied natural gas terminals, restart coal plants temporarily, and preside over Germany's final nuclear shutdown in April 2023 while arguing it should perhaps have been delayed. A 2024 backlash against a botched home-heating law showed how quickly climate policy costs can be mobilized against incumbents. The accumulated lesson is neither that governing greens always sell out nor that they transform everything, but that they reliably shift the policy frontier, renewables targets, phase-out dates, nature protection budgets, while absorbing disproportionate blame for the compromises any coalition requires, and that their survival depends on institutional depth, not charisma alone.

sections.heading: Green Parties Across the World's Electoral Systems
sections.body: Where green parties thrive is to a first approximation a question of electoral engineering. Systems of proportional representation with modest thresholds, common across continental Europe, let a party polling five to fifteen percent convert votes into seats, patronage, and media standing; majoritarian first-past-the-post systems strangle the same vote share. The contrast is stark between Germany, where the Greens have been a governing party at every level, and the United Kingdom, where the Green Party of England and Wales polled over a million votes in 2015 yet held a single seat in the House of Commons, finally rising to four seats in 2024. New Zealand's switch from first-past-the-post to mixed-member proportional representation in 1996 transformed its Greens from perennial outsiders into a parliamentary fixture and, after 2017, a governing partner. In the United States, plurality voting plus restrictive ballot-access laws confine the Green Party founded in 1984 to protest candidacies; Ralph Nader's 2000 presidential run, 2.7 percent nationally and some 97,000 votes in a Florida decided by 537, convinced many American progressives that third-party environmentalism was worse than futile, and pushed environmental energy into the Democratic coalition and nonparty groups instead. Australia's preferential voting spares green voters the spoiler trap: the Australian Greens, led for years by the Tasmanian doctor Bob Brown, have used Senate proportionality to hold balance-of-power positions and in 2010 supported the Gillard government's short-lived carbon price. Scandinavia and the Benelux countries maintain multiple green or green-left parties; Latin America's greens range from Mexico's PVEM, widely criticized as green in name only, to Colombia's Alianza Verde; the Greens/EFA group in the European Parliament peaked at seventy-four seats after the 2019 green wave election before falling back in 2024. Beyond party competition, green politics lives inside other movements where party channels are blocked. Kenya's Green Belt Movement, founded by Wangari Maathai in 1977, planted tens of millions of trees while training women in civic action, work that earned Maathai the 2004 Nobel Peace Prize, the first awarded for environmental leadership. In authoritarian settings, environmentalism has often been a licensed outlet that turned subversive: Bulgaria's Ecoglasnost and the Baltic movements against Soviet industrial projects in the late 1980s became seedbeds of national democratic revolutions. China permits environmental NGOs limited space while suppressing independent organization, channeling policy through the party-state's own ecological civilization program. The general rule that emerges is twofold: proportional rules plus post-materialist electorates, young, urban, educated, produce durable green parties, while everywhere else green politics adapts by colonizing existing parties, courts, bureaucracies, and streets, which is why measuring the movement by party vote share alone always understates it. Political scientists led by Ronald Inglehart tied the underlying demand to post-materialism itself: generations raised in material security shift their priorities from income and order toward self-expression and environmental quality, which predicts both where green parties rise first and why economic crises temporarily deflate their vote.

sections.heading: Movements, NGOs, and Direct Action
sections.body: Party politics is only the visible peak of political environmentalism; beneath it operates a dense ecology of organizations with distinct theories of change. The oldest layer is the conservation establishment: the Sierra Club from 1892, the Royal Society for the Protection of Birds from 1889, the National Audubon Society, the World Wide Fund for Nature founded in 1961, and the International Union for Conservation of Nature, which maintains the Red List of threatened species. These groups work through land purchase, science, lobbying, and litigation, and command memberships in the millions. A second layer was born of 1970s confrontation. Greenpeace began in 1971 when activists sailed an old fishing boat, the Phyllis Cormack, from Vancouver toward the Amchitka nuclear test site in Alaska, inventing the media-savvy direct action, small boats between harpoon and whale, climbers on smokestacks, that made it a global brand now claiming some three million supporters; the French secret service's 1985 sinking of its ship Rainbow Warrior in Auckland harbor, killing the photographer Fernando Pereira, only cemented its stature. Friends of the Earth, founded in 1969 by David Brower after he split from the Sierra Club over nuclear power, grew into a decentralized federation active in over seventy countries. Earth Day 1970 begat professionalized law-and-science shops like the Natural Resources Defense Council and the Environmental Defense Fund, which pioneered suing agencies into enforcing their own statutes. A more radical layer rejects both lobbying and spectacle: Earth First!, founded in 1980 under the slogan no compromise in defense of Mother Earth, practiced tree-sits and road blockades, and the clandestine Earth Liberation Front carried out arson against ski resorts and SUV dealerships in the 1990s and 2000s, tactics the mainstream movement condemned and which American authorities prosecuted as terrorism. Grassroots environmentalism of livelihood, distinct from all of these, has often come from the global South: India's Chipko movement of the 1970s, in which Himalayan villagers, many of them women, embraced trees to stop logging; Brazil's rubber tappers led by Chico Mendes, assassinated in 1988, whose struggle created extractive reserves in the Amazon; and the Ogoni campaign against oil pollution in the Niger Delta, whose leader Ken Saro-Wiwa was hanged by Nigeria's military regime in 1995. The 2010s added networked mass movements: 350.org's divestment campaign, which by the early 2020s had secured divestment commitments from institutions holding tens of trillions of dollars in assets; Greta Thunberg's 2018 school strike, which within a year mobilized an estimated six million people in a single week of climate strikes; and Extinction Rebellion's mass civil disobedience in London in April 2019, followed by controversial disruption tactics from successor groups like Just Stop Oil. The strategic argument among all these wings, does disruption win sympathy or squander it, remains empirically unsettled, with studies pointing in both directions, but historically the movement's victories have usually required both the radicals who made the issue unavoidable and the insiders who wrote the resulting rules.

sections.heading: The Ideological Family: Deep Ecology to Ecosocialism
sections.body: Green politics is a family of ideologies rather than a single doctrine, and its internal arguments are as instructive as its shared commitments. The deepest divide runs between anthropocentric and ecocentric foundations. Deep ecology, named by the Norwegian philosopher Arne Naess in 1973, holds that nonhuman life has value independent of its usefulness to people and calls for a substantial reduction in human impact; Naess contrasted it with shallow environmentalism that merely manages pollution for human benefit. Its critics, notably the social ecologist Murray Bookchin, accused deep ecology of misanthropy and argued instead that ecological destruction flows from social hierarchy and domination, so that dismantling hierarchy, through decentralized, directly democratic municipalism, is the precondition of ecological sanity; Bookchin's ideas later influenced the Kurdish movement in northern Syria. Ecofeminism, developed by thinkers such as Val Plumwood, Carolyn Merchant, and Vandana Shiva, connects the domination of nature with the domination of women, arguing that both rest on the same dualisms of reason over nature and men over women, and points to the empirical pattern that women, who fetch water and grow food across much of the world, bear the first costs of ecological collapse. Ecosocialism, associated with writers like André Gorz, James O'Connor, and John Bellamy Foster, locates the root cause in capitalism's growth imperative: firms that must expand to survive will always externalize costs onto nature, so ecological stability requires social ownership and planning; Foster reconstructs from Marx a theory of metabolic rift between society and soil. At the opposite pole, free-market environmentalism and green conservatism argue that secure property rights, tort liability, and price signals protect nature better than bureaucracies, pointing to the fisheries where tradable quotas ended collapse, and drawing on the conservative intuition, articulated by Roger Scruton, that conservation is the natural politics of those who love settled places. Between the poles sits ecological modernization, the reigning philosophy of most governing greens and mainstream parties alike, which holds that economic growth can be decoupled from environmental harm through technology, regulation, and green investment; its evidence is that many rich countries have cut territorial emissions while growing, and its critics reply that global decoupling remains far too slow and partly an artifact of offshoring production. Bright green optimism about technology, associated with ecomodernists who embrace nuclear power, dense cities, and intensive agriculture to spare land for nature, faces degrowth, articulated by Serge Latouche, Tim Jackson, and Jason Hickel, which argues that rich economies must deliberately shrink material throughput and redistribute, because sufficient absolute decoupling has never been observed at the required pace. These quarrels are not academic decoration; they decide real platforms, whether a green party supports nuclear plants, carbon markets, or growth itself, and every practical green program is a negotiated treaty among these tendencies.

sections.heading: Environmental Justice and the Global South
sections.body: For much of its first century, organized environmentalism was demographically narrow, and the environmental justice movement arose to force the question of who bears environmental burdens. Its American founding moment came in 1982 in Warren County, North Carolina, where a poor, majority-Black county was chosen to receive soil laced with polychlorinated biphenyls; more than five hundred protesters were arrested lying before the trucks. The 1987 report Toxic Wastes and Race in the United States, directed by Benjamin Chavis for the United Church of Christ, found race to be the single strongest predictor of living near commercial hazardous waste facilities, stronger than income, and the sociologist Robert Bullard's Dumping in Dixie documented the pattern across the South. The First National People of Color Environmental Leadership Summit in 1991 adopted seventeen Principles of Environmental Justice, and in 1994 President Clinton's Executive Order 12898 directed every federal agency to address disproportionate impacts on minority and low-income populations. Landmark cases kept the issue alive: the lead poisoning of Flint, Michigan's water supply after a 2014 cost-saving switch, and the petrochemical corridor along the lower Mississippi known as Cancer Alley. Globally the same logic scales up. The doctrine of common but differentiated responsibilities, written into the 1992 Rio conventions, acknowledges that industrialized countries caused the great majority of cumulative emissions, the United States and Europe together account for roughly half of all carbon dioxide emitted since 1750, while the poorest countries suffer first and worst from the consequences. The concept of climate justice therefore demands finance and technology transfer, embodied in the rich world's 2009 Copenhagen pledge of one hundred billion dollars a year by 2020, met only around 2022, and in the loss-and-damage fund agreed at the Sharm el-Sheikh conference in 2022 after three decades of small-island advocacy. Scholars such as Joan Martínez-Alier describe an environmentalism of the poor: thousands of conflicts, catalogued in the EJAtlas database he co-founded, in which peasant, fishing, and indigenous communities defend land and water against mines, dams, plantations, and pipelines, not from post-material sentiment but because their subsistence depends on it. The costs are lethal: the watchdog Global Witness has documented roughly two hundred killings of land and environmental defenders each year through the late 2010s and early 2020s, with Colombia, Brazil, the Philippines, and Honduras among the deadliest countries, the murdered Honduran river defender Berta Cáceres in 2016 being emblematic. Indigenous peoples, roughly five percent of humanity, steward lands holding a large share of remaining biodiversity, and campaigns such as Standing Rock in 2016 against the Dakota Access pipeline fused indigenous rights with climate politics. Environmental justice has reshaped green politics itself, pushing parties and NGOs to treat equity not as an add-on but as the test of whether an environmental policy is legitimate at all.

sections.heading: Building the International Climate Regime
sections.body: No environmental problem exposes the machinery of international politics like climate change, because the atmosphere is a single commons and every ton of carbon dioxide mixes globally within about a year. The scientific foundations are old: Joseph Fourier described the greenhouse effect in 1824, John Tyndall measured the heat-trapping gases in 1859, Svante Arrhenius calculated in 1896 that doubling atmospheric carbon dioxide would warm the planet by several degrees, and Charles David Keeling's measurements from Mauna Loa, begun in 1958, drew the ascending curve that made the process visible. Politics caught up in 1988, when NASA's James Hansen testified to the United States Senate during a heat wave that warming had begun, and governments created the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change to assess the science. The 1992 Rio Earth Summit produced the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change, ratified by essentially every state, with the objective of preventing dangerous anthropogenic interference with the climate system and the equity principle of common but differentiated responsibilities. The 1997 Kyoto Protocol translated this into binding emission targets averaging about five percent below 1990 levels for industrialized countries, with tradable permits and offset mechanisms; the United States Senate had preemptively voted 95 to 0 against joining any treaty exempting developing countries, and never ratified. Kyoto's architecture, targets for some and not others, could not accommodate the rise of China, whose emissions passed America's around 2006, and the 2009 Copenhagen summit collapsed in acrimony. What replaced it was a different design. The 2015 Paris Agreement, adopted by 196 parties, binds every country procedurally rather than substantively: each submits a nationally determined contribution, updates it every five years under a ratchet expectation, and reports transparently, while the treaty sets collective goals of holding warming well below two degrees Celsius and pursuing efforts toward 1.5 degrees. The 2018 IPCC special report on 1.5 degrees sharpened the timetable, popularizing the finding that global emissions must fall roughly forty-five percent by 2030 and reach net zero around 2050 for a reasonable chance at the lower target, and net-zero pledges spread until they covered most of world output, of very uneven credibility. The United States withdrew under President Trump, rejoined under President Biden in 2021, and announced withdrawal again in 2025, illustrating the regime's exposure to domestic swings. Assessment must be double-entry. Before Paris, plausible trajectories pointed toward roughly four degrees of warming by 2100; current policies point toward something near 2.5 to 3, and full implementation of pledges lower still, while actual emissions kept setting records into the mid-2020s and the 1.5 degree threshold is, on current physics, nearly out of reach. The regime has manifestly bent the curve and just as manifestly not yet bent it enough, and both facts are essential to an honest account.

sections.heading: Policy Instruments: Pricing, Regulating, Subsidizing
sections.body: Environmental policy is a toolbox, and green politics in office is largely the craft of choosing and combining tools. The oldest tool is command-and-control regulation: the state sets technology or performance standards, bans substances, and licenses polluters. Its triumphs are real, catalytic converters, unleaded gasoline, scrubbers on power plants, the phase-out of ozone-destroying chlorofluorocarbons under the 1987 Montreal Protocol, often called the most successful environmental treaty ever, and its weakness is rigidity: a uniform standard ignores that abatement is cheap for some firms and dear for others. Economists since Arthur Pigou in 1920 have therefore urged pricing: tax each unit of pollution at the damage it causes, and let every actor find their own cheapest way to avoid it. Finland and Sweden introduced the first carbon taxes in 1990; Sweden's has risen above one hundred euros per ton while its economy grew, and British Columbia's 2008 revenue-neutral carbon tax became a textbook case. The rival market instrument is cap-and-trade: the state fixes a total quantity of allowed emissions, auctions or allocates permits, and lets trade discover the price. The United States acid rain program of 1990 cut sulfur dioxide far more cheaply than predicted, inspiring the European Union Emissions Trading System of 2005, which after early over-allocation and price collapses was reformed with a market stability reserve and by the early 2020s priced carbon at eighty to one hundred euros per ton, with measurable effects on coal generation. By 2024 the World Bank counted around seventy-five carbon pricing schemes covering roughly a quarter of global emissions, most at prices well below estimates of social damage, and the political economy remains treacherous: France's 2018 fuel-tax increase ignited the gilets jaunes protests and was withdrawn, teaching that carbon pricing survives only when revenues visibly return to households, as with Canada's rebate design, or fund alternatives people can actually use. Subsidy tools push from the other side: German feed-in tariffs and later reverse auctions drove renewable costs down a learning curve of roughly twenty percent per doubling of deployment, and the 2022 United States Inflation Reduction Act, mobilizing several hundred billion dollars in clean-energy tax credits, marked a deliberate turn toward green industrial policy, matched by the European Green Deal's regulatory-plus-investment package aiming at a fifty-five percent emissions cut by 2030. Complementary instruments fill the corners: border carbon adjustments to stop industry relocating to unpriced jurisdictions, which the EU began phasing in from 2023; efficiency standards for buildings, vehicles, and appliances; deposit-refund schemes; payments for ecosystem services, as in Costa Rica, which reversed deforestation while growing tourism; and procedural tools like environmental impact assessment and freedom-of-information rules that arm civil society. The consistent empirical lesson is that instrument wars are sterile; durable decarbonization episodes, Britain's coal exit, Scandinavian heating, combine a price, a regulation, an investment, and a political compensation mechanism, because each tool covers another's flank.

sections.heading: Green Political Theory: Time, Nature, and Democracy
sections.body: Beneath the daily policy fights, green politics raises questions that strain the foundations of political theory. The first is time. Democracies answer to living voters on electoral cycles of two to five years, but climate and biodiversity decisions bind people who cannot vote because they are not yet born. Philosophers formalize the problem through discounting: a standard economic discount rate of five percent makes a harm suffered in one century appear about 130 times smaller than the same harm today, which is why the 2006 Stern Review's choice of a near-zero pure time preference, yielding urgent action, and William Nordhaus's higher market-based rates, yielding gradualism, produced opposite prescriptions from similar physics. Greens generally side with Stern: pure time preference between generations is, in their view, ethically arbitrary. Institutional inventions try to give the future a voice: Wales created a Future Generations Commissioner under its 2015 Well-being of Future Generations Act, Finland's parliament runs a Committee for the Future, and constitutional courts have begun enforcing intertemporal fairness, as when Germany's Federal Constitutional Court ruled in 2021 that a climate law postponing most emission cuts past 2030 unconstitutionally offloaded freedom-destroying burdens onto the young. The second question is standing: who or what counts? Christopher Stone's 1972 essay Should Trees Have Standing proposed legal rights for natural objects, an idea that migrated from law-review provocation to statute: Ecuador's 2008 constitution grants rights to Pachamama, nature itself; Bolivia passed a Law of Mother Earth in 2010; New Zealand's 2017 Te Awa Tupua Act made the Whanganui River a legal person with appointed guardians, fusing Māori cosmology with Western legal form; Colombian courts extended personhood to the Atrato River and parts of the Amazon. Litigation has become a central green instrument: the Dutch Urgenda case ordered the state in 2019 to cut emissions twenty-five percent as a human-rights duty, Germany's Neubauer judgment followed, and in 2024 the European Court of Human Rights found Switzerland's climate inaction violated the Convention in a case brought by elderly Swiss women. The third question is whether democracy itself is up to the task. In the 1970s, ecological pessimists like Robert Heilbroner and William Ophuls speculated that scarcity would require authoritarian rationing, and some today point enviously at China's administrative capacity. The green mainstream draws the opposite conclusion, backed by empirical work showing democracies generally outperform autocracies on environmental quality: the remedy for democratic short-termism is more democracy, deeper and slower, citizens' assemblies like France's 2019 Convention for Climate and Ireland's assembly, deliberative bodies chosen by lot that have repeatedly proven more ambitious than parliaments, participatory budgeting, and strong local self-government. That wager, that ecological limits and self-government can be reconciled, is the philosophical heart of green politics, and it remains a wager, not a theorem.

sections.heading: Opposition, Skepticism, and Backlash
sections.body: Green politics has always generated counter-politics, and understanding the opposition is part of understanding the field. The most consequential form has been organized doubt. Internal documents show that Exxon's own scientists modeled global warming with impressive accuracy from the late 1970s, while from the 1990s the company and industry coalitions funded think tanks and publicists who magnified uncertainty; historians Naomi Oreskes and Erik Conway documented in Merchants of Doubt how a handful of Cold War physicists moved from defending tobacco to attacking climate science using the same playbook, doubt is our product, as a tobacco memo once put it. The Global Climate Coalition lobbied against Kyoto until its corporate members began defecting around 2000; the fight then shifted from denying warming to delaying policy, what researchers now call discourses of delay: someone else's fault, technology will fix it, policy will hurt the poor, our share is too small to matter. A second form is distributional revolt. Carbon pricing and regulation concentrate visible costs on identifiable groups, drivers, farmers, coal regions, while spreading benefits thinly across everyone and into the future, a configuration political scientists recognize as maximally explosive. France's gilets jaunes erupted in 2018 over a fuel surtax layered on rural cost-of-living stress; Dutch farmers, facing court-ordered nitrogen cuts, spawned a protest party, the BoerBurgerBeweging, that topped a provincial election in 2023; and a European farmers' revolt in 2024 pushed Brussels to shelve pesticide rules. Populist radical-right parties have made climate policy a signature enemy, fusing it with resentment of urban elites, the German AfD campaigns against wind turbines and heat pumps, and the term greenlash entered political vocabulary in the mid-2020s as center-right parties also retreated from net-zero commitments they had recently endorsed. A third form is intellectual critique that greens must take seriously on its merits. Bjørn Lomborg's The Skeptical Environmentalist argued in 2001 that many environmental trends were improving, that climate policy often fails cost-benefit tests against health and poverty spending; the ecomodernist Breakthrough Institute accuses mainstream environmentalism of romantic hostility to the nuclear power and intensive agriculture that could actually spare nature; and development economists warn that rich countries which industrialized on coal have no standing to deny poor ones cheap energy, a charge sharpened whenever European banks refuse to finance African gas projects. Empirically, public opinion surveys, such as the UN Development Programme's Peoples' Climate Vote covering fifty countries, find large majorities calling climate change an emergency even in many fossil-fuel states, but willingness to pay is shallower than concern, and support drops sharply when policies carry visible personal price tags. The strategic implication that successful green politicians have drawn is that climate policy fails as sacrifice and survives as tangible improvement, warm homes, cheap transit, good jobs, and that ignoring the distributional question does not make it disappear; it makes it someone else's weapon.

sections.heading: Current Frontiers: Green Deals, Just Transition, and Adaptation
sections.body: The green politics of the 2020s is organized around a handful of frontier ideas. The first is the marriage of climate policy with economic renewal under the banner of green new deals. The phrase, consciously echoing Franklin Roosevelt, was floated by the columnist Thomas Friedman in 2007 and by a British economists' group in 2008, but became a mass political project when Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Senator Edward Markey introduced a Green New Deal resolution in the United States Congress in February 2019, pairing decarbonization with job guarantees and public investment. The resolution never passed, but its logic, climate policy as industrial strategy and social contract rather than austerity, migrated into the 2022 Inflation Reduction Act's clean-energy manufacturing credits and into the European Green Deal announced in 2019, with its Just Transition Fund for coal regions. Just transition itself, a term coined in the 1990s by the American labor leader Tony Mazzocchi to demand that workers displaced by environmental policy be made whole, is now treaty language in the Paris Agreement's preamble and hard cash in deals like the eighty-five-billion-rand package assembled for South Africa's coal belt. The second frontier is adaptation, long the neglected half of climate policy because it looked like admitting defeat. With roughly 1.2 degrees of warming already delivering record heat waves, floods like Pakistan's 2022 inundation that covered a third of the country, and intensifying wildfire seasons, planning for consequences has become unavoidable: sea walls and managed retreat, heat action plans of the kind Ahmedabad pioneered for India after its 2010 heat disaster, drought-resilient agriculture, and early-warning systems the UN aims to extend to every person. Adaptation raises its own justice problems, since protection follows property values unless politics intervenes. The third frontier is the extension of green politics into new domains: circular-economy law attacking waste through right-to-repair rules and producer responsibility; the 2022 Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework's pledge to protect thirty percent of land and sea by 2030; food politics, since the global food system drives roughly a quarter to a third of emissions and most deforestation; and a revived population-free focus on consumption, since the richest ten percent of humanity accounts for close to half of consumption emissions. The fourth frontier is contested technology: whether solar geoengineering research should proceed at all, how to govern carbon dioxide removal, and the divide over nuclear power, which splits green parties country by country, Finland's Greens endorsed it in 2022 while Germany's completed its abolition. Behind all of these run the youth and litigation movements, Fridays for Future's strikes and a docket of climate cases that passed two thousand worldwide by the mid-2020s, which together have shifted the argument from whether to act to who pays, how fast, and who decides, which is where green politics always ends up.

sections.heading: Failure Modes, Limits, and Hard Lessons
sections.body: An honest account of political environmentalism must catalogue its characteristic failures, because they are systematic rather than accidental. The first failure mode is symbolic politics: targets without mechanisms. Governments have repeatedly adopted distant goals, carbon neutrality by 2050, thirty percent protected land, while declining the near-term measures arithmetic requires; the gap between pledge and policy, tracked annually in the UN Environment Programme's Emissions Gap Report, is the movement's central frustration. Related is greenwashing, the corporate counterfeit of environmental performance, from carbon offsets that pay for forests never at risk, investigations in 2023 found a large majority of one major registry's rainforest credits delivered little real benefit, to net-zero pledges resting on accounting rather than abatement; regulators have begun responding with green-claims directives and securities disclosure rules. The second failure mode is the spoiler and blame trap of party politics: in majoritarian systems green candidacies can elect the most anti-environmental option, as Florida in 2000 taught, while in coalition systems junior green partners absorb outsized blame for compromise, as Ireland in 2011 showed. The third is the distributional blind spot: policies designed by cost-benefit spreadsheets but experienced as an attack on rural livelihoods or working-class budgets reliably generate backlash that sets the cause back further than inaction would have, the gilets jaunes lesson. Fourth is the rebound problem: efficiency gains partly self-cancel as savings are re-spent, an effect William Stanley Jevons noticed about coal in 1865, which is why efficiency policy needs caps or prices behind it. Fifth is leakage and offshoring: a jurisdiction that prices carbon while importing carbon-intensive goods has partly exported, not eliminated, its footprint, the problem border carbon adjustments attempt to close. Sixth is institutional capture and simple corruption, from regulators staffed by the regulated to green subsidies harvested by fraud. Against these stand equally systematic lessons from the victories, acid rain, the ozone layer, leaded gasoline, the renewable cost collapse. Durable wins combined a scientifically undeniable harm, a visible alternative technology, a policy that concentrated benefits and diffused costs rather than the reverse, and an enforcement mechanism that survived changes of government. They were also usually incremental in form and radical in effect: the Montreal Protocol began with a modest freeze and tightened on a ratchet as evidence and industry capability grew. For the citizen or practitioner asking what to do when green politics goes wrong, the record therefore suggests: audit claims against delivered tons and hectares, not announcements; design compensation before imposing costs; build coalitions that include labor, farmers, and industry incumbents who can profit from the transition; prefer ratchets to one-shot bargains; and keep separate books for what is politically feasible and what is physically sufficient, because confusing the two, in either direction, is how both denial and despair are manufactured. The distance between those two ledgers is the true state of green politics at any moment.

guides.title: Marxism & Communism
guides.summary: A full account of Marxist theory and communist practice: the philosophy of history, the economics of value and crisis, the theory of class and the state, the major branches from Leninism to Western Marxism, the regimes built in its name, and the strongest criticisms made of it.

sections.heading: Why This Subject Matters and What It Actually Claims
sections.body:
Few bodies of thought have moved as much of the world as Marxism. At its high-water mark around 1980, states governed by parties claiming descent from Karl Marx ruled roughly a third of humanity, from Berlin to Hanoi. The doctrine reorganised the property systems of the Russian Empire, China, Eastern Europe, Korea, Indochina, Cuba and much of the decolonising world; it shaped the twentieth century's most destructive conflicts and its most consequential famines; and its analytical vocabulary — class, ideology, exploitation, alienation, mode of production — entered ordinary speech so thoroughly that people who reject every one of Marx's conclusions still argue in his terms.

Understanding it properly requires holding two things apart that are constantly conflated. The first is Marxism as an analytical system: a theory of how societies are structured by their arrangements for producing material life, how those arrangements generate conflicting interests, and how they change over time. The second is communism as a political movement and a set of actually existing states. The two are related but not identical, and no serious study collapses them. A person may accept much of Marx's account of how capitalism works while rejecting everything the Soviet Union did, and many prominent Marxists did exactly that. Equally, one cannot treat the regimes as a mere accident unrelated to the theory, because they were built by people who had read the theory closely and believed they were applying it.

What does Marxism actually claim? At its core, four propositions. First, that the way a society produces and distributes the material necessities of life is the deepest determinant of its politics, law, culture and consciousness — not the only cause, but the foundation on which the rest is raised. Second, that in every society since the dissolution of primitive communal life, this production has been organised so that one group appropriates a surplus produced by another, generating antagonistic classes with irreconcilable interests. Third, that capitalism, though enormously productive and historically progressive compared to feudalism, contains internal contradictions that periodically throw it into crisis and that tend, over long periods, to undermine it. Fourth, that the working class, created and concentrated by capitalism itself, has both the interest and the eventual capacity to abolish class society altogether, producing a classless, stateless order in which production is consciously and collectively directed.

Each of these claims has been fiercely contested for a century and a half, and the honest position is that the record is mixed. The first proposition has been enormously fertile as a research programme even for non-Marxists. The fourth has, so far, no successful instance. Reading Marx as scripture or as refuted nonsense both prevent understanding. He was a nineteenth-century thinker of extraordinary power who got some things strikingly right, some things badly wrong, and left ambiguities that his followers resolved in radically different and sometimes catastrophic directions.

sections.heading: Marx and Engels: The Lives Behind the Texts
sections.body:
Karl Marx was born in Trier, in the Prussian Rhineland, on 5 May 1818, into a comfortable family of rabbinical descent whose father had converted to Lutheranism to keep his legal practice. He studied law at Bonn, then philosophy at Berlin, where he fell in with the Young Hegelians — radical readers of the philosopher G. W. F. Hegel who turned Hegel's system against religion and the Prussian state. His doctorate, on the atomism of Democritus and Epicurus, was awarded by Jena in 1841. Barred from an academic career by his politics, he turned to journalism, editing the Rheinische Zeitung until Prussian censorship closed it in 1843.

Exile followed: Paris in 1843, Brussels in 1845, briefly back to Germany during the 1848 revolutions, and from 1849 to his death in 1883, London. There he lived in genuine poverty for years, sustained by journalism for the New-York Daily Tribune and by the money of Friedrich Engels. Three of his six children died in childhood, and the household's misery is documented in a Prussian police spy's report of 1852 describing two rooms of broken furniture and thick dust. He spent his days in the British Museum Reading Room, working through parliamentary Blue Books, factory inspectors' reports and the whole of classical political economy.

Friedrich Engels, born in Barmen in 1820, was the indispensable partner. Son of a textile manufacturer with mills in Manchester, he was sent to work in the family firm and used the position to document what he saw, producing The Condition of the Working Class in England in 1845 — a work of pioneering social investigation, with mortality statistics, housing descriptions and wage data, written when he was twenty-four. He then spent decades running a business he despised in order to fund Marx, and after Marx's death edited the unfinished second and third volumes of Capital from a mass of manuscripts. Engels was the more accessible writer, and much of what the world received as "Marxism" — including the systematising, more deterministic formulations in Anti-Dühring and Socialism: Utopian and Scientific — is Engels's rendering.

The principal texts form a rough sequence. The Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844, unpublished until 1932, contain the theory of alienation. The German Ideology, written 1845–46 and also long unpublished, sets out historical materialism. The Communist Manifesto of February 1848, commissioned by the Communist League, is the great agitational statement, perhaps thirty pages, written when Marx was twenty-nine. The Eighteenth Brumaire of Louis Bonaparte, 1852, is his finest piece of concrete political analysis. The Grundrisse, notebooks of 1857–58, was unpublished until 1939. Capital, Volume I, appeared in 1867; Volumes II and III were assembled posthumously by Engels in 1885 and 1894. The Critique of the Gotha Programme, 1875, contains his most explicit remarks on a future society.

sections.heading: Historical Materialism: Base, Superstructure and Modes of Production
sections.body:
Historical materialism is the philosophical core: an account of what drives historical change. Marx's starting point is deliberately unglamorous. Human beings must eat, be clothed and be sheltered before they can do anything else, so the way a society organises the production of these necessities is the most basic fact about it. In the preface to A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy (1859) he gives the most compressed statement: in the social production of their existence, people enter into definite relations independent of their will, relations of production corresponding to a given stage of the development of their material productive forces; the totality of these relations constitutes the economic structure of society, the real foundation on which arises a legal and political superstructure and to which correspond definite forms of social consciousness.

Two terms carry the weight. The forces of production are the means available for making things: tools, machines, techniques, accumulated know-how, the trained capacities of workers, the land and raw materials. The relations of production are the social arrangements governing who controls those means and who gets what is produced — slavery, serfdom, wage labour, and the property law that codifies each. A mode of production is a matched pair of forces and relations: the ancient slave mode, the feudal mode, the capitalist mode.

The engine of change is a mismatch between the pair. Productive forces tend to develop — knowledge accumulates, techniques improve. Relations of production, being entrenched in law, custom and the interests of a ruling class, are sticky. At some point the relations that once fostered growth become, in Marx's word, fetters upon it. Then, he writes, an epoch of social revolution begins. Feudal guild restrictions and manorial obligations, which had once organised production, became obstacles to manufacture and trade, and were broken by a rising bourgeoisie over several centuries in Europe.

The base–superstructure metaphor has caused endless trouble, and the trouble is real rather than a misreading by hostile critics. Read strictly, it says law, politics, religion, philosophy and art are determined by economics, which is plainly too crude — the Reformation, the codification of Roman law, the rise of nationalism are not straightforwardly readable off production techniques. Engels himself, in letters of 1890 to Joseph Bloch and 1894 to Heinz Starkenburg, insisted that the economic element is determining only "in the last instance", that superstructural elements exert real reciprocal influence, and that he and Marx had over-stressed the economic side polemically against opponents who ignored it entirely. Later Marxists have spent enormous effort on this problem, and the more sophisticated versions treat the base as setting limits and probabilities rather than dictating outcomes. The unhelpfully strong version — economic determinism — is the one most often attacked and least often held by careful readers.

sections.heading: The Labour Theory of Value and the Origin of Surplus
sections.body:
Marx's economics begins from a puzzle inherited from Adam Smith and David Ricardo: what determines the ratio in which commodities exchange? A coat trades for twenty yards of linen; what makes those quantities equivalent? Marx argues that behind every exchange ratio lies a common substance, and that the only thing all commodities share is that they are products of human labour. The value of a commodity is therefore determined by the socially necessary labour time required to produce it — "socially necessary" meaning under normal conditions of production with the average skill and intensity prevailing. If a lazy tailor takes twice as long, his coat is not worth twice as much.

Marx distinguishes use-value, the concrete usefulness of a thing, from exchange-value, its ratio against other commodities. The tension between them animates his whole analysis: capitalism produces use-values only incidentally, as a by-product of pursuing exchange-value.

The decisive move is the theory of surplus value, which he regarded as his own contribution. The puzzle is where profit comes from. If commodities exchange at their values, nobody gains by trading, since equivalents change hands. Profit cannot arise from cheating in the market, because what one gains another loses and total profit would be zero. The solution is that the capitalist buys one very peculiar commodity: labour power, the worker's capacity to work, which is bought for a day, a week or a month. Like every commodity, labour power has a value determined by what it costs to produce and reproduce — the food, housing, clothing, training and family maintenance needed to keep a worker alive and replaced. But labour power has the unique property that its use creates value, and it can be made to create more value than it costs.

Suppose the goods a worker needs each day embody six hours of socially necessary labour. That is the value of a day's labour power, and it is what the wage buys, honestly and at full value. But the working day is not six hours; it is ten, or twelve. In the first six hours the worker reproduces the value of his own wage — necessary labour. In the remaining hours he produces surplus value, which the capitalist appropriates because he owns the product. Exploitation, in Marx's technical sense, means precisely this unpaid portion of the working day. It is not fraud. It is the normal operation of a system in which one class owns the means of production and the other owns only its capacity to labour.

Marx defines the rate of surplus value, or rate of exploitation, as surplus labour divided by necessary labour — in the example, four over six, about 67 per cent. He distinguishes absolute surplus value, raised by lengthening the working day, from relative surplus value, raised by cheapening workers' subsistence through productivity growth so that necessary labour shrinks. The nineteenth-century struggle over the ten-hour day, and the twentieth-century productivity drive, map onto this distinction exactly.

sections.heading: Capital, Accumulation and the Dynamics of Crisis
sections.body:
Capital, for Marx, is not a thing but a process: money thrown into circulation in order to return as more money. He writes the circuit as M–C–M′, money buys commodities which are sold for a larger sum. This contrasts with simple commodity circulation, C–M–C, where a weaver sells cloth to buy bread and the process ends in consumption. The capitalist circuit has no natural stopping point. The surplus must be reinvested, because a capitalist who does not accumulate is overtaken by one who does. Competition, not personal greed, enforces this: it is a structural compulsion.

The consequences unfold across Capital. Accumulation drives mechanisation, since a firm that introduces machinery produces more cheaply than the social average and captures extra profit until competitors copy it. Mechanisation raises what Marx calls the organic composition of capital, the ratio of constant capital — machinery, buildings, raw materials, symbol c — to variable capital, wages, symbol v. Constant capital transfers its value to the product but adds none; only living labour creates new value. If the rate of surplus value s/v stays constant while c grows relative to v, the rate of profit, defined as s/(c+v), must fall. This is the law of the tendential fall in the rate of profit, set out in Volume III, and Marx himself listed counteracting tendencies: raising the rate of exploitation, cheapening the elements of constant capital, foreign trade, and the depression of wages below the value of labour power. Whether the tendency dominates the counter-tendencies is disputed to this day, and the empirical evidence is genuinely equivocal.

Marx also identifies a reserve army of labour. Mechanisation continually expels workers, and this pool of unemployed disciplines those in work and holds wages down. When accumulation is rapid the reserve army shrinks and wages rise, squeezing profits; investment falls, the reserve army refills, and wages fall again. This is a theory of cycles, and Marx observed roughly decennial industrial cycles in Britain across his lifetime — 1825, 1836, 1847, 1857, 1866.

Crisis in Marx is not a malfunction but a normal, recurrent purging. Overaccumulation means too much capital relative to profitable outlets. Crises destroy capital values through bankruptcy, write-downs and idle plant, restoring profitability and permitting a new upswing. Marx also notes the possibility of realisation crises: capitalists collectively pay workers less than the value of what is produced, so the workers cannot buy back the whole product, and the surplus must find buyers elsewhere. This underconsumptionist strand was developed by Rosa Luxemburg and, in a different key, influenced Keynes.
