conflict. That argument is unresolved and its resolution will do much to determine what the word means a
generation from now.

sections.heading: Conservatism Beyond the West
sections.body:
Treating conservatism as a European invention exported elsewhere obscures a great deal. Every society with
a long institutional history has produced arguments for preserving it, and several of those arguments are
older than Burke and were developed with more philosophical elaboration.

Confucian political thought, systematised from the teachings of Kong Fuzi in the fifth century before the
common era and dominant in imperial China for two millennia, is conservative in a recognisable sense. It
grounds order in ritual propriety and in reciprocal duties within hierarchical relationships, treats the
family as the model for political authority, holds that rulers legitimate themselves through virtue and
performance rather than through consent, and regards the transmission of a classical canon as the core of
education. Its influence on political culture in China, Korea, Japan, Vietnam and Singapore remains
substantial. Lee Kuan Yew's arguments in the 1990s about Asian values, holding that social order and
collective welfare should take priority over individual rights claims, drew explicitly on this inheritance,
and were contested just as explicitly by Asian democrats who regarded the framing as a convenient defence of
incumbent power.

Islamic political thought contains an equally developed traditionalist strand, resting on the authority of
revealed law, the consensus of scholars and the practice of the early community. It is essential to
distinguish traditional religious conservatism, which defends established schools of jurisprudence and
customary practice, from twentieth-century Islamist movements, which are frequently revolutionary in method
and modernist in organisation, seeking to remake the state according to an ideological programme. Many
traditional scholars have opposed those movements precisely on conservative grounds.

Hindu, Japanese and African traditions each have comparable strands: defence of caste and inherited
religious practice in one case, of imperial continuity and Shinto observance in another, of customary law,
lineage and chieftaincy in many African polities where colonial and postcolonial states overlaid but never
replaced older structures.

Two general observations follow. First, conservatism outside the West often confronts a problem that
European conservatives did not face in the same form: the tradition to be conserved was disrupted by
colonial rule, so conservative politics becomes entangled with anti-colonial nationalism and with disputes
about which of several available pasts counts as authentic. That entanglement makes labels imported from
European political history fit badly.

Second, the label is frequently used carelessly by outside commentators to mean religiously observant, or
authoritarian, or simply opposed to Western liberal norms, and these are different things that do not
reliably travel together. A careful reader should ask, of any group described as conservative, what
specifically it seeks to conserve, by what authority, and against what alternative, rather than assuming
that the answers resemble those familiar from Britain or America.

sections.heading: Criticisms, Internal Tensions and Limits
sections.body:
Conservatism attracts serious objections, and a fair account must state them at their strongest rather than
in caricature. Several also come from within the tradition.

The oldest criticism is that conservatism has functioned historically as the defence of privilege dressed in
philosophical clothing. Its arguments about accumulated wisdom, unintended consequences and the fragility of
order were deployed against the abolition of slavery, against extending the vote beyond property owners,
against votes for women, against trade union rights, against desegregation and against decolonisation. In
each case the predicted catastrophe did not arrive and the reform is now defended by conservatives
themselves. The pattern is documented enough that it demands an answer, and the honest conservative answer
is that prudential arguments are contingent and can be wrong, which concedes that the disposition provides
no guarantee of being right.

Albert Hirschman analysed the recurring forms of the argument in The Rhetoric of Reaction in 1991,
identifying three theses that appear across two centuries of opposition to reform: perversity, that the
change will produce the opposite of its aim; futility, that it will change nothing; and jeopardy, that it
will endanger some previous achievement. His point was not that these are always false, since sometimes
they are true, but that their automatic deployment regardless of the case suggests rhetoric rather than
analysis.

A second criticism is the indeterminacy problem. If the principle is to conserve, what is to be conserved
when the inheritance contains contradictory elements, or when the recent past was itself revolutionary?
Conservatives in post-communist states faced exactly this and answered in incompatible ways. The
practical consequence is that conservatism cannot by itself decide the questions that matter most, and must
import substantive commitments from elsewhere, whether religious, national or liberal.

A third is that the tradition has no stable account of when change is warranted. Burke supported the
American Revolution and the Glorious Revolution while condemning the French one, and the criteria he offered
for distinguishing them are debated by scholars to this day.

The internal tensions are equally real. Free markets dissolve the communities traditionalists defend.
National sovereignty conflicts with international commerce. Populist majoritarianism conflicts with
constitutional restraint. Religious conservatism conflicts with secular libertarianism in the same
coalition. These are not failures of tidiness; they are substantive disagreements about ends.

What survives all this, and what even sympathetic critics tend to grant, is the epistemic core: complex
social arrangements encode information their participants cannot fully articulate, reforms have consequences
their designers do not foresee, institutions are easier to destroy than to build, and legitimacy depends on
continuity as well as on justification. Those claims are defensible on their own terms and are supported by
a good deal of unhappy twentieth-century experience. They establish a burden of proof and a case for
caution. They do not establish that any particular thing should be preserved, and treating them as if they
did is the characteristic failure of the tradition.

guides.title: Socialism
guides.summary: A full account of socialism as an idea and as a practice: its definitions and disputes, its origins, the Marxian analysis at its core, the calculation debate, its major branches from social democracy to anarchism to command planning, its record in government, and the criticisms and replies that continue to define the argument.

sections.heading: Defining a Contested Word
sections.body:
Socialism is a family of political and economic doctrines united by the claim that the means of producing goods and services should be owned or controlled collectively — by society, by the state, by workers, or by communities — rather than privately by individuals who hire labour for wages. Beyond that core, the word covers arrangements so different from one another that arguments conducted with it frequently talk past each other, and a reader needs to know from the outset that no single definition commands agreement.

The disputes are substantive rather than semantic. One concerns the object of collective control: is it the whole economy, or only "the commanding heights" of banking, energy, transport and heavy industry, or only natural monopolies? A second concerns the agent: the central state, regional government, workers in each enterprise, consumers in cooperatives, or society as an undifferentiated whole? A third concerns the mechanism of coordination: administrative planning, markets in which the firms happen to be collectively owned, or a moneyless system of direct allocation? A fourth concerns method: revolution or elections. A fifth concerns the endpoint: for Marx, socialism was a transitional stage after which the state itself would wither away into communism, whereas for most social democrats the mixed economy is not a waystation but the destination.

Because of this, several familiar oppositions are unreliable. "Socialism versus communism" is used one way by Marxists, for whom communism is the later, higher, stateless stage, and another way in Cold War popular usage, where socialism meant the milder Western welfare states and communism the Soviet bloc. "Socialism versus capitalism" implies a binary that no real economy has ever occupied: every developed country runs a mixed economy in which the state's share of GDP ranges from roughly 25 to over 55 per cent and where large sectors — usually roads, courts, defence, basic education and much of health care — are collectively provided as a matter of course.

It is also worth separating three things that are often conflated. Ownership concerns who holds legal title and residual claims. Control concerns who actually makes decisions, which regulation can shift without changing title. Distribution concerns who ends up with the output, which taxes and transfers can reshape without touching either. A country can have high redistribution with almost entirely private ownership, as Denmark broadly does, or state ownership with harshly unequal distribution, as several nominally socialist states have done. Programmes described as socialist have targeted all three levers in different combinations.

Finally, the word carries an enormous emotional charge that varies by country. In much of Europe, Latin America and India it names an ordinary parliamentary tradition with a century of governing experience. In the United States it has functioned since the early twentieth century largely as a term of political abuse, applied to policies that European conservatives take for granted. Understanding what someone means requires knowing which tradition and which country's usage they are drawing on.

sections.heading: Origins Before Marx: Utopians, Owenites and the Early Movement
sections.body:
The word socialisme appears in French around 1832 in the Saint-Simonian journal Le Globe and in English at roughly the same date among the followers of Robert Owen. The ideas are older. Communal ownership appears in Plato's Republic for the guardian class, in the early Christian community described in Acts, in monastic rules, in the sixteenth-century Anabaptist experiments at Münster, in Thomas More's Utopia of 1516, and in the Diggers led by Gerrard Winstanley who occupied St George's Hill in Surrey in 1649 and declared the earth a common treasury.

What made the nineteenth century different was industrialisation. Between roughly 1780 and 1850 in Britain, and later elsewhere, the factory system concentrated enormous numbers of propertyless wage workers in cities under conditions that shocked contemporary observers of every political stripe. Child labour from age six, working days of 14 to 16 hours, life expectancy in Manchester in the 1840s recorded at around 26 years for labourers against about 38 nationally, and periodic mass unemployment during trade slumps created a visible social question that older political vocabularies could not address.

Three figures dominate the early response, later labelled the utopian socialists by Friedrich Engels in his 1880 pamphlet Socialism: Utopian and Scientific — a label that was polemical and somewhat unfair. Henri de Saint-Simon (1760-1825) argued that society should be run by industrialists, engineers and scientists on rational, productive principles rather than by an idle aristocracy, and that the government of men would give way to the administration of things. Charles Fourier (1772-1837) designed elaborate cooperative communities called phalanstères, each of 1,620 people organised so that work matched individual passions; roughly 30 Fourierist communities were founded in the United States, almost all failing within a decade. Robert Owen (1771-1858), a genuinely successful mill-owner, ran New Lanark in Scotland with an eight-hour day and free schooling while turning a profit, then poured his fortune into New Harmony, Indiana, which collapsed in about two years.

Alongside these ran a more combative current. Pierre-Joseph Proudhon published What Is Property? in 1840, answering his own question with "property is theft" while defending small producers' possession against large accumulation, and became the founding figure of anarchism. Louis Blanc argued in 1839 for state-financed "social workshops" and coined the formula, later attributed to Marx, that society should draw "from each according to his abilities, to each according to his needs" — the phrase in fact originates with Blanc and earlier with Étienne-Gabriel Morelly.

The revolutions of 1848 across Europe, in which socialist demands appeared briefly in government in France before the June Days massacre, marked the movement's first entry into national politics and its first defeat. The immediate lesson drawn across the Continent was that moral appeal and model communities would not suffice against organised state power, and that whatever came next would need a theory of how existing society actually worked.

sections.heading: Marx and Engels: The Analysis That Reorganised the Movement
sections.body:
Karl Marx (1818-1883) and Friedrich Engels (1820-1895) did not invent socialism, and they were not the first to advocate collective ownership. Their contribution was a theory that claimed to explain why capitalism produced the misery its critics described, why it would generate the class capable of ending it, and why it would eventually fail on its own terms. That claim to scientific status — that socialism followed from an analysis of how the existing system works rather than from a moral blueprint — is what allowed Marxism to displace rival socialisms across most of the Continent by 1900.

The framework has several interlocking parts. Historical materialism holds that the way a society organises production — its "mode of production" — conditions its politics, law, religion and ideas. History moves through successive modes: primitive communism, ancient slave societies, feudalism, capitalism, and eventually socialism. Transitions occur when the productive forces available, meaning technology and human skill, outgrow the property relations that organise them, at which point the relations become "fetters" and are burst apart in a period of social revolution. This is a structural theory, not a moral one; Marx was frequently scathing about socialists who argued from justice.

Class is defined by relationship to the means of production, not by income or status. Under capitalism the bourgeoisie owns productive property; the proletariat owns nothing but its capacity to work and must sell it to live. This is a relation, not a ranking, and it generates antagonism structurally rather than through the malice of individual employers, most of whom Marx regarded as themselves compelled by competition.

The most influential single text remains The Communist Manifesto, written for the Communist League and published in February 1848, weeks before the revolutions broke out. Its opening claim that "the history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggles" and its closing appeal to the workers of all countries defined how the movement saw itself. Its ten-point programme is instructive because much of it now sounds unremarkable: a progressive income tax, abolition of inheritance, free public education, centralisation of credit and transport in state hands.

Capital, whose first volume appeared in 1867, is the analytical core, with volumes two and three assembled by Engels from Marx's notes after his death. It is a study of capitalism's internal logic, not a description of socialism; Marx wrote almost nothing about how a socialist economy would actually run, dismissing such exercises as "writing recipes for the cookshops of the future." That silence is not incidental. It left his successors with a powerful critique and almost no institutional design, and much of the twentieth century consists of attempts to fill the gap.

sections.heading: Value, Surplus and Crisis: The Mechanism of the Marxian Critique
sections.body:
The engine of Marx's economics is the labour theory of value, inherited from Adam Smith and David Ricardo and then turned against their conclusions. In this framework the value of a commodity is determined by the socially necessary labour time required to produce it under average conditions of skill and intensity. "Socially necessary" is doing real work in that sentence: a slow or incompetent producer does not thereby create more value, and a technological improvement that halves the labour needed halves the value of the product even for firms still using old methods.

The crucial move concerns labour power. Marx distinguishes labour, the activity, from labour power, the capacity to work that the worker sells. Like any commodity, labour power has a value equal to the labour time needed to reproduce it — the food, housing, training and family maintenance that keep a worker alive and replaceable. But its use value to the employer is that it can produce more value than it costs. If subsistence requires the equivalent of four hours of work and the working day is ten hours, six hours are surplus, appropriated by the owner. This surplus value, in Marx's account, is the sole source of profit, interest and rent, and it is extracted not by cheating but through an exchange in which the worker is paid the full market value of what is sold.

From this Marx derives several tendencies. The rate of surplus value can be raised by lengthening the working day (absolute surplus value) or by cheapening subsistence goods through productivity growth (relative surplus value), which explains capitalism's relentless technological dynamism. Competition drives firms to substitute machinery for labour, raising what Marx calls the organic composition of capital. Since only labour produces surplus, a rising ratio of machinery to labour implies a tendency for the rate of profit to fall, offset by countervailing factors including cheaper inputs, higher exploitation and foreign expansion. Crises of overproduction recur because the drive to accumulate outruns the purchasing power of workers whose wages are held down by that same drive.

The theory faces serious technical difficulties, which honest exposition should state. The transformation problem — converting labour values into observed market prices when profit rates equalise across industries of differing capital intensity — was identified by Marx himself in volume three and has never been resolved to general satisfaction, despite substantial literatures on both sides. Eugen von Böhm-Bawerk's critique of 1896 remains the standard statement of the objection. The marginalist revolution of the 1870s, associated with William Stanley Jevons, Carl Menger and Léon Walras, replaced labour-value theory in mainstream economics with subjective marginal utility, and virtually no academic economist today uses the labour theory of value as a price theory.

What has proved more durable is the underlying sociological insight: that the employment relation involves an asymmetry of power, that the intensity and length of work are contested, and that unemployment functions as a disciplining device. These claims are testable, are widely tested, and survive without the value theory.

sections.heading: The Socialist Calculation Debate
sections.body:
If a society abolishes private ownership of productive assets and therefore markets for them, how does it decide what to produce and by what methods? This is the single most important technical question ever posed to socialism, and the argument about it ran from 1920 to the present.

Ludwig von Mises opened it in a 1920 article, expanded into Socialism in 1922. His claim was not that planners would be lazy or corrupt but that rational calculation would be logically impossible. Choosing between two production methods requires comparing the value of the inputs they consume in alternative uses. That comparison requires prices for capital goods. Prices for capital goods emerge from competitive bidding by owners risking their own property. Abolish the ownership and you abolish the bidding, hence the prices, hence the possibility of knowing whether building a railway with steel and concrete costs society more or less than the alternatives. Production would proceed by guesswork.

The first reply came from Oskar Lange in 1936-37 and Abba Lerner, proposing "market socialism" or the competitive solution. A Central Planning Board would set prices by trial and error, instructing state managers to produce where marginal cost equals price and to minimise cost, then raise prices for goods in shortage and lower them for goods in surplus. Lange argued this replicated the Walrasian auctioneer of general equilibrium theory more faithfully than real capitalism, since the board could adjust without the waste of business cycles. For a generation this was widely regarded as having settled the matter in socialism's favour.

Friedrich Hayek reformulated the objection in a way that has worn far better, most influentially in "The Use of Knowledge in Society" (1945). His point was epistemological rather than computational. The knowledge required to run an economy is not a set of data waiting to be collected; it is dispersed, tacit, local and often unarticulated — the particular circumstances of time and place known only to the man on the spot, the hunch about a supplier, the sense that a machine is about to fail. Prices are not merely coordinating signals but a mechanism for economising on knowledge nobody possesses in full. A planning board cannot gather what nobody has written down, and much of it would not survive being written down. Hayek added a dynamic point: markets are a discovery procedure that generates new knowledge through competition, and a system that only allocates known resources efficiently misses what matters.

The computational strand has revived with modern technology. Advocates including Paul Cockshott and Allin Cottrell argued in the 1990s that input-output planning of an economy with millions of products is now tractable, since sparse-matrix iterative methods scale far better than solving the full system of simultaneous equations would suggest. Critics respond that the binding constraint was never arithmetic but the quality and honesty of the input data, and that preferences and technologies are not stable coefficients waiting to be measured. The debate is genuinely unresolved.

sections.heading: The Great Split: Reform, Revolution and 1914
sections.body:
By 1900 the socialist movement was large, disciplined and international. The German Social Democratic Party (SPD) was the model: founded in 1875, illegal under Bismarck's anti-socialist laws from 1878 to 1890, it nonetheless won 34.8 per cent of the vote and became the largest party in the Reichstag in 1912, with a million members, its own newspapers, choirs, cycling clubs and funeral societies. The Second International, founded in Paris in 1889, coordinated parties across Europe and beyond and made May Day an international workers' holiday.

Beneath the growth ran an unresolved contradiction. The party's formal Marxism predicted capitalist collapse and revolution; its actual practice was electoral, parliamentary and increasingly successful within the existing order. Eduard Bernstein confronted this directly in Evolutionary Socialism (1899), arguing from the statistics that Marx's predictions were failing — the middle classes were growing rather than being proletarianised, capital ownership was spreading through joint-stock companies, wages were rising and crises were not intensifying. He concluded that socialism should be pursued through incremental reform and that "the movement is everything, the final goal nothing." This "revisionism" was formally condemned by the SPD but described what the party in fact did.

Karl Kautsky held the orthodox centre: revolution was inevitable but should be awaited rather than provoked, and the party's task was to build strength. On the left, Rosa Luxemburg answered Bernstein in Reform or Revolution (1900), insisting reforms were valuable but could not accumulate into socialism because they left the property relation untouched. Vladimir Lenin, in What Is To Be Done? (1902), argued that workers left alone develop only "trade union consciousness" and that a disciplined vanguard party of professional revolutionaries was required — a claim about organisation that would define twentieth-century communism.

The break came in August 1914. The International had repeatedly resolved that workers would not fight one another in a capitalist war. On 4 August the SPD deputies voted for war credits; French, Austrian and British socialists did likewise. The internationalist commitment collapsed within days, and the movement never reunified. Those who opposed the war gathered at Zimmerwald in Switzerland in 1915 and formed the nucleus of a new movement.

The Russian Revolution of 1917 completed the rupture. After Lenin's Bolsheviks took power in October, the founding of the Third International (Comintern) in 1919 imposed twenty-one conditions on member parties, including expulsion of reformists and adoption of the Bolshevik model. Socialist parties across Europe split, in Germany with a bitterness compounded by the Social Democratic government's use of the Freikorps to crush the Spartacist rising in January 1919 and the murder of Luxemburg and Karl Liebknecht. From that point socialism and communism were separate, hostile movements, and the enmity between them materially assisted the rise of fascism.

sections.heading: Social Democracy and the Construction of the Welfare State
sections.body:
The reformist branch became the most consequential socialist tradition by the simple measure of how many people have lived under governments it formed. Its method is electoral, its instruments are taxation, regulation, public services, macroeconomic management and collective bargaining, and its stated goal shifted over the twentieth century from replacing capitalism to civilising it.

Sweden supplies the paradigm. The Social Democratic Party governed almost continuously from 1932 to 1976 — 44 years, the longest democratic tenure of any party in the world. The Saltsjöbaden Agreement of 1938 between the trade union confederation LO and the employers' federation established a framework of centralised bargaining without state interference that lasted decades. The Rehn-Meidner model, formulated in 1951, deliberately combined solidaristic wage policy, meaning equal pay for equal work regardless of the employer's profitability, with active labour market policy to retrain workers displaced when unprofitable firms failed. The design pushed low-productivity firms out of business on purpose and moved workers into high-productivity ones, which is why Sweden combined compressed wages with rapid growth.

Britain's post-war settlement was more statist. The Attlee government elected in 1945 nationalised the Bank of England, coal, civil aviation, telecommunications, railways, road haulage, electricity, gas and steel — roughly 20 per cent of the economy — and founded the National Health Service in July 1948 on the principle of care free at the point of use, funded from general taxation. The Beveridge Report of 1942, which sold 600,000 copies, framed the programme as an attack on "five giants": want, disease, ignorance, squalor and idleness.

Germany's SPD formally abandoned Marxism at Bad Godesberg in 1959, accepting markets with the slogan "as much competition as possible, as much planning as necessary," and became a governing party. France's Parti Socialiste under François Mitterrand won in 1981 on a radical programme of nationalisations and reflation, then executed the "tournant de la rigueur" in 1983 when capital flight and franc devaluation forced a reversal — a widely cited demonstration of the constraints on national social democracy in an open economy.

The tradition's achievements are large and measurable. Between 1945 and 1975 Western European economies grew at 4 to 5 per cent annually, inequality fell to historic lows, and universal health coverage, pensions and education were established. Its difficulties emerged with the stagflation of the 1970s, when the Phillips curve trade-off broke down, and with capital mobility after the collapse of the Bretton Woods system in 1971-73, which made it harder to tax mobile capital or run independent monetary policy. The "Third Way" of Tony Blair and Gerhard Schröder in the late 1990s accepted much of the market-liberal settlement while retaining redistribution, a move its supporters call realism and its critics call capitulation. That argument is still live.

sections.heading: Marxism-Leninism and the Command Economy in Practice
sections.body:
The Soviet model is the most consequential socialist experiment by any measure, and any serious treatment must describe both what it built and what it cost, without softening either.

Its institutional core was the command economy, established after the New Economic Policy's partial market restoration was ended in 1928. Gosplan, the State Planning Committee, drew up five-year plans setting output targets for roughly 20,000 to 25,000 product categories at the aggregate level, disaggregated by ministries into millions of specific assignments. Prices were administratively set and did not clear markets. Enterprises were judged on physical output targets, which generated the model's most notorious pathologies: factories producing nails by weight made a few huge ones, factories judged by count made tiny useless ones, quality was neglected because it was unmeasured, and managers systematically understated capacity to secure achievable targets, a practice called the ratchet effect.

The achievements were nonetheless real. The USSR industrialised faster than any country had previously: industrial output multiplied several-fold in the 1930s while the West was in depression, urbanisation rose from about 18 per cent in 1926 to over 60 per cent by the 1980s, literacy went from roughly 40 per cent to near-universal, and the country produced the industrial base that defeated the Wehrmacht, launched Sputnik in 1957 and put Yuri Gagarin in orbit in 1961. Life expectancy roughly doubled between 1917 and the 1960s.

The costs were catastrophic. Forced collectivisation of agriculture from 1929 destroyed the peasant economy and produced famine in 1932-33 in which excess deaths are estimated at 5 to 7 million across the USSR, with roughly 3.5 to 5 million in Ukraine, where the Holodomor is recognised by many states as genocide. The Great Terror of 1937-38 executed approximately 680,000 people according to NKVD records opened after 1991. The Gulag system held around 1.5 to 2.5 million prisoners at its peak in the early 1950s, with total deaths in the camps generally estimated between 1.5 and 1.8 million. China's Great Leap Forward from 1958 to 1962 produced a famine with credible death estimates ranging from 15 to 45 million, the deadliest in recorded history. Cambodia under the Khmer Rouge from 1975 to 1979 killed perhaps 1.5 to 2 million out of a population of 8 million.

Whether these outcomes follow from socialism as such or from the specific combination of one-party dictatorship, war, backwardness and terror is the central historical dispute. Anti-communist writers, including Hayek in The Road to Serfdom (1944), argued that comprehensive planning requires suppressing dissent because plans cannot survive democratic revision. Democratic socialists reply that the movement's own members were among the first victims, that social democracies achieved comparable growth without terror, and that no theoretical link runs from public ownership to mass killing. Both positions have serious advocates and the question is not settled by assertion.

sections.heading: Anarchism, Syndicalism and the Libertarian Left
sections.body:
A substantial socialist tradition rejected the state entirely, holding that the coercive apparatus of government could not be an instrument of liberation because it reproduces domination whoever holds it. This tradition lost the argument organisationally in the nineteenth century and has periodically returned.

Mikhail Bakunin (1814-1876) was Marx's principal antagonist in the First International, expelled at the Hague Congress of 1872 in a split that destroyed the organisation. Bakunin's prediction is much quoted because it reads as prophetic: a "dictatorship of the proletariat" would become a dictatorship over the proletariat by a new class of ex-workers turned rulers, "the most vile and terrible lie our century has created." Peter Kropotkin (1842-1921), a Russian prince turned geographer, supplied the constructive theory in The Conquest of Bread (1892) and Mutual Aid (1902), the latter arguing from field zoology that cooperation is at least as important an evolutionary factor as competition.

Anarcho-syndicalism made the trade union rather than the party the vehicle. The strategy was to build revolutionary unions capable of running industry, then seize it through a general strike. Its high point was Spain, where the Confederación Nacional del Trabajo reached over a million members by 1936. During the Civil War, following the July 1936 coup, workers in Catalonia and Aragon collectivised roughly 70 per cent of the workforce in Barcelona, running trams, telephones, textile mills and much of agriculture through assemblies and elected committees. George Orwell's Homage to Catalonia describes it from inside. The collectives functioned for two to three years under wartime conditions, then were destroyed by Franco's victory in 1939 and, earlier, suppressed by Communist forces in the May Days of 1937 in Barcelona. Historians disagree sharply about their economic performance, and the wartime setting makes clean judgement impossible.

Council communism, associated with Anton Pannekoek and Herman Gorter, proposed workers' councils — soviets in the original, pre-Bolshevik sense — as the organ of both revolution and government, rejecting both parliaments and vanguard parties. Councils appeared spontaneously in Russia in 1905 and 1917, Germany in 1918-19, Hungary in 1956 and Poland in 1980-81, which suggests something recurrent about the form.

Guild socialism, a British current associated with G. D. H. Cole in the 1910s and 1920s, proposed national guilds of workers managing each industry with the state representing consumers, an explicit attempt to avoid both the market and the bureaucracy. It never held power but its arguments recur in every subsequent debate about workers' control.

More recently, libertarian socialist ideas have informed the Zapatista autonomous municipalities in Chiapas since 1994 and the administration of northeast Syria after 2012, both of which combine assembly democracy with cooperative production under severe external pressure.

sections.heading: Market Socialism and Worker Cooperatives
sections.body:
A persistent middle position holds that the objectionable feature of capitalism is not markets but the private ownership of capital and the wage relation, and that both can be changed while retaining prices, competition and consumer choice. This family of proposals aims squarely at the calculation objection by keeping the mechanism that objection defends.

Yugoslavia ran the most extensive national experiment. After the split with Stalin in 1948, Tito's regime introduced workers' self-management from 1950: enterprises were "social property" belonging to no one in particular, managed by elected workers' councils that chose directors, set wages and decided investment, while competing in markets. The system produced strong growth in the 1950s and 1960s, averaging around 6 per cent annually, and considerable genuine participation. It also produced characteristic distortions predicted by the theoretical literature, especially the Ward-Domar-Vanek result that a firm maximising income per worker rather than total profit has a perverse incentive to shed members rather than expand, contributing to persistent unemployment that reached over 15 per cent by the 1980s alongside labour emigration. Soft budget constraints — the phrase is János Kornai's — meant loss-making firms were bailed out, and inflation spiralled in the 1980s before the state disintegrated in war.

The Mondragón Corporation in the Basque Country is the most successful surviving cooperative complex, founded in 1956 by the priest José María Arizmendiarrieta with five workers making paraffin heaters. It now comprises around 95 cooperatives with roughly 70,000 employees and annual revenues in the range of 11 billion euros. Its rules are instructive: members buy a capital stake, one member has one vote regardless of stake, and the internal pay ratio between lowest and highest was historically capped near 1:6 and now runs to roughly 1:9, against ratios of several hundred to one in comparable listed firms. Its own bank, Caja Laboral, and its university supply capital and skills that cooperatives usually struggle to obtain. Its limits are real too: many overseas subsidiaries employ conventional wage workers who are not members, and the flagship appliance cooperative Fagor went bankrupt in 2013 with 5,600 jobs lost.

Theoretical designs abound. John Roemer's "coupon socialism" would give every citizen an equal, non-transferable portfolio of shares in all firms, keeping stock markets and managerial discipline while preventing concentration. David Schweickart's "economic democracy" combines worker-managed firms, social control of investment through a capital assets tax, and markets for goods but not for capital or labour. Rudolf Meidner's Swedish wage-earner funds of 1976 proposed transferring 20 per cent of large firms' profits annually into union-controlled funds, gradually shifting ownership; it was diluted almost beyond recognition before enactment in 1983 and abolished in 1991, and is frequently cited as the point at which Swedish social democracy stopped advancing.

sections.heading: Democratic Socialism and the Nordic Question
sections.body:
"Democratic socialism" names a position that insists on both terms: full political democracy with competitive elections and civil liberties, and a decisive shift in economic ownership or control away from private capital. Its adherents distinguish it from social democracy, which they characterise as managing capitalism rather than transcending it, though the boundary between the two is blurred in practice and many people use the labels interchangeably.

The Nordic countries are the perennial reference point, and the argument about them is instructive precisely because both sides get something right. Denmark, Sweden, Norway, Finland and Iceland combine very high tax-to-GDP ratios — Denmark's has run around 46 per cent, against roughly 27 per cent in the United States — with universal health care, tuition-free universities, generous parental leave of a year or more, and near-universal childcare. Union density is high, historically 60 to 90 per cent, and most wages are set by collective agreement rather than statutory minimum wage, which several of these countries do not have at all.

Yet by conventional measures of economic freedom these are strongly market economies. Denmark and Sweden rank near the top of international indices for ease of doing business, property rights protection and openness to trade. State ownership of industry is modest outside Norway's oil sector, where Equinor and the sovereign wealth fund built from petroleum revenue, worth well over a trillion US dollars, represent the largest genuinely socialised asset in any market democracy. Danish labour market policy is explicitly "flexicurity": employers can dismiss workers easily, and the state provides high unemployment benefits and intensive retraining.

So the honest answer to "are the Nordics socialist?" depends on the definition adopted at the outset. If socialism means social ownership of the means of production, they are not, and their own prime ministers have said so — Denmark's Lars Løkke Rasmussen told a Harvard audience in 2015 that Denmark is "a market economy" and asked not to be called socialist. If socialism means decommodifying essential goods so that access does not depend on ability to pay, they have gone further than almost anywhere. Both statements are true and they are not in contradiction.

Two further cautions are warranted. Nordic outcomes rest on preconditions that are hard to export: small, historically homogeneous populations of 5 to 10 million, very high institutional trust, low corruption, strong state capacity built over centuries, and in Norway's case extraordinary resource wealth. Attempts to attribute results wholly to policy design underrate this. And the model has been under pressure: Sweden's school voucher reforms of 1992 introduced for-profit providers, tax rates have fallen from 1980s peaks, and the countries' Gini coefficients have risen since the 1990s, though from a very low base and still well below Anglo-American levels.

sections.heading: Socialism Beyond Europe: Anti-Colonial and Developmental Variants
sections.body:
Outside Europe, socialism was adopted less as a response to industrial capitalism — which barely existed in most colonies — than as a programme for national independence and rapid development. This changed its content substantially, and produced results that resist simple summary.

African socialism took several forms. Julius Nyerere's Tanzania, from the Arusha Declaration of 1967, pursued ujamaa, meaning familyhood, grounded in a claim that pre-colonial African societies were already communal. The programme nationalised banks and major industries and, from 1973, moved roughly 5 to 9 million people into planned villages, initially voluntarily and later by force. Its social results were striking: adult literacy rose from around 30 per cent to over 70 per cent, and primary enrolment approached universality. Its economic results were poor: agricultural output fell, food imports rose, and by 1985 Tanzania was among the world's poorest countries and dependent on aid. Nyerere himself acknowledged the villagisation coercion as a mistake. Kwame Nkrumah's Ghana, Sékou Touré's Guinea and Modibo Keïta's Mali followed variants with broadly similar mixes of educational gains and economic difficulty.

India after independence adopted a non-aligned democratic socialism: the term "socialist" was inserted into the constitution's preamble by the Forty-second Amendment in 1976. The Nehruvian model combined five-year plans, a large public sector in heavy industry, and extensive licensing of private investment — the "Licence Raj" — with continuing private ownership, elections and a free press. Growth averaged about 3.5 per cent annually from 1950 to 1980, the so-called Hindu rate of growth, and accelerated sharply after liberalisation from 1991.

Latin America produced both electoral and revolutionary versions. Salvador Allende's Popular Unity government in Chile, elected in 1970 with 36.6 per cent of the vote, nationalised copper and much of banking before being overthrown by the coup of 11 September 1973, with documented United States support for destabilisation. Cuba after 1959 built health and education systems that produce infant mortality and literacy figures comparable to or better than much richer countries, while sustaining a one-party state, severe restrictions on expression and movement, and an economy dependent first on Soviet subsidy and later on tourism and remittances, further constrained by the United States embargo in force since 1962.

China represents the largest single transformation. From 1978 Deng Xiaoping's reforms decollectivised agriculture through the household responsibility system, opened special economic zones and admitted foreign investment while retaining Communist Party rule and state control of finance, land and strategic industry. The result — several hundred million people lifted above extreme poverty lines within a generation — is the largest reduction in absolute poverty in recorded history. Whether the system is socialist, state capitalist or something without a good name is disputed by everyone including its own theorists, whose official term is "socialism with Chinese characteristics" and whose practice combines a private sector generating most employment with a party that appoints the leadership of the largest firms.

sections.heading: New Left, Feminist and Ecological Currents
sections.body:
From the 1960s onward, socialism was substantially reworked by movements that found the classical account too narrow, arguing that focusing on the wage relation alone left major forms of domination unexplained and unaddressed.

The New Left emerged after 1956, a year in which Khrushchev's secret speech denounced Stalin and Soviet tanks crushed the Hungarian uprising, discrediting the official communist parties for a generation of Western intellectuals. Its characteristic themes — alienation, culture, bureaucracy, everyday life — drew on Marx's early Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844, published only in 1932, and on Antonio Gramsci's prison writings, which introduced hegemony: the idea that ruling classes maintain power principally through consent manufactured in civil society, in schools, churches and media, rather than through coercion. Herbert Marcuse's One-Dimensional Man (1964) argued that affluent capitalism neutralised opposition by satisfying manufactured needs. The Frankfurt School more broadly shifted socialist attention from the factory to the culture industry.

Socialist feminism developed the domestic labour debate of the 1970s, asking how unpaid household work fits an analysis built around wage labour. The observation is straightforward and was largely absent from classical accounts: the reproduction of labour power — bearing and raising children, cooking, cleaning, nursing the sick — is indispensable to any economy and has overwhelmingly been performed by women without pay. Wages for Housework, launched by Selma James and Mariarosa Dalla Costa in 1972, demanded payment; others argued that demand would entrench the division of labour rather than abolish it. Heidi Hartmann's essay "The Unhappy Marriage of Marxism and Feminism" (1979) argued that class analysis absorbed feminism rather than integrating it, and that patriarchy has a material basis independent of capitalism. Modern time-use surveys give the debate quantitative teeth: unpaid work is typically estimated at 10 to 40 per cent of GDP depending on valuation method, and women perform roughly two to three times as much of it as men in most countries measured.

Ecological socialism, or eco-socialism, holds that endless accumulation is incompatible with a finite biosphere and that environmental crisis and class exploitation share a root. Murray Bookchin's social ecology from the 1960s argued that the domination of nature originates in the domination of humans by humans. André Gorz, James O'Connor and more recently Kohei Saito have developed the strand, with Saito's reading of Marx's late ecological notebooks arguing for "degrowth communism." The tradition is not unopposed on the left: "ecomodernists" and many trade unionists argue that growth funded the welfare state and that decarbonisation requires massive industrial expansion in renewables, nuclear and grids rather than contraction. This disagreement about growth is currently one of the sharpest inside socialist politics, and it has no agreed resolution.

sections.heading: 1989-1991 and the Aftermath
sections.body:
The collapse of the Soviet bloc between 1989 and 1991 was the largest single political event in socialism's history and remains the reference point against which every subsequent argument is conducted.

The proximate causes were economic stagnation and political liberalisation interacting. Soviet growth rates, plausibly 5 to 6 per cent annually in the 1950s, had fallen to near zero by the early 1980s. The economy could produce steel and rockets but not consumer goods, software or reliable food distribution; queueing was a daily fact and shortage a structural feature rather than an accident, as Kornai's work on the "economics of shortage" demonstrated. Oil prices, which had funded imports through the 1970s, collapsed from around 35 dollars a barrel in 1980 to under 15 by 1986. Military spending consumed an estimated 15 to 25 per cent of GDP against roughly 6 per cent in the United States. Mikhail Gorbachev's perestroika from 1985 attempted restructuring and glasnost permitted criticism; the combination removed fear without producing improvement.

The sequence was rapid. Poland's semi-free elections in June 1989 gave Solidarity every seat it was allowed to contest. Hungary opened its border with Austria in August. The Berlin Wall opened on 9 November. Czechoslovakia's Velvet Revolution followed in November and December, Romania's Ceaușescu was executed on 25 December, and the USSR itself dissolved on 26 December 1991 after a failed August coup.

The transition that followed is itself a major case study. "Shock therapy" — rapid price liberalisation, privatisation and fiscal contraction, advised by Western economists including Jeffrey Sachs — produced in Russia a collapse in output of roughly 40 per cent between 1991 and 1998, hyperinflation exceeding 2,500 per cent in 1992, and a fall in male life expectancy from about 64 years to 57 by 1994, an increase in mortality that demographers estimate at millions of excess deaths. The loans-for-shares scheme of 1995-96 transferred major assets to a small group at a fraction of value, creating the oligarchy. Poland, which combined rapid reform with retained social protection and had a large private agricultural sector already, fared considerably better and returned to pre-1989 output within about five years. Whether the difference was sequencing, institutions or initial conditions is still argued.

For socialism as a movement the effect was ideological as much as material. Francis Fukuyama's "The End of History?" (1989) captured a widespread sense that liberal democracy plus markets was the terminal form. Western social democratic parties moved right; the SPD's Schröder and Labour's Blair explicitly repositioned. Interest revived after the financial crisis of 2007-09, which discredited claims about market self-correction, and again around inequality after Thomas Piketty's Capital in the Twenty-First Century (2013) documented the long-run tendency of capital returns to exceed growth. Membership of avowedly socialist organisations rose substantially in the United States and Britain during the 2010s, though from a very low base.

sections.heading: The Standing Criticisms and the Replies
sections.body:
A serious account has to set out the strongest objections and the strongest answers, since the argument has been running for 175 years and neither side has run out of material.

The incentive objection holds that if reward is separated from contribution, effort falls. Without the threat of loss and the prospect of gain, managers do not innovate, workers do not exert themselves, and no one accepts the discomfort of change. The evidence from command economies broadly supports the concern regarding innovation and quality, less so regarding raw output growth in the extensive phase of industrialisation. Socialists answer that intrinsic motivation, professional pride and collective purpose are real and empirically robust motivators, that most people in capitalist economies are already salaried employees without residual claims, and that cooperatives such as Mondragón and the John Lewis Partnership sustain productivity comparable to conventional firms. The honest position is that incentives matter but are not exhausted by money, and that the design of any system has to take both seriously.

The knowledge objection, from Hayek, is that no central body can gather dispersed and tacit information. This has proved the most durable criticism, and market socialists concede it by keeping prices. Advocates of planning answer that large corporations already plan internally on a scale exceeding many national economies — Walmart's internal logistics allocate more resources than the Soviet Union did for many product categories — and that modern data systems change the constraint. Critics reply that firms plan inside a price environment they did not create, which is the whole point.

The power objection, associated with Hayek and with anarchists from Bakunin onward, holds that concentrating economic and political power in one apparatus removes the check that each provides on the other. The twentieth-century record gives this real force. Democratic socialists answer that concentration is a feature of one-party rule rather than of public ownership, and that private concentration is itself a form of unaccountable power — that a firm is an authoritarian institution its employees cannot vote in, a point developed by Elizabeth Anderson in Private Government (2017).

The socialist case against markets rests on several claims that market defenders also take seriously: that market outcomes reflect purchasing power rather than need, so resources flow to luxury goods while basic needs go unmet; that competition generates negative externalities, of which climate change is the largest; that labour markets clear at wages set partly by the fear of destitution; that inherited wealth makes initial positions arbitrary; and that instability is endemic, with financial crises recurring roughly every decade. Market defenders answer that regulation, taxation and social insurance can address each without abolishing the price mechanism — which is, in effect, the social democratic programme, and explains why that programme has been the most durable.

sections.heading: Reading the Argument Honestly: Failure Modes and Open Questions
sections.body:
Several habits of thought reliably corrupt discussion of socialism, and a reader can improve their own judgement considerably by watching for them.

The first is the no-true-socialism move, which insulates the doctrine from evidence by declaring every failed case not really socialist. It has a legitimate core — the Soviet Union genuinely did not resemble what most nineteenth-century socialists advocated, and neither Bakunin nor Luxemburg would have recognised it as their goal — but deployed reflexively it makes the position unfalsifiable. The symmetrical error on the other side is to treat every socialist proposal as identical to Stalinism, which collapses a hundred years of bitter internal argument into a single object. Both moves are ways of avoiding the harder question of which specific institutional arrangements produce which specific outcomes.

The second is the definitional switch mid-argument. A great deal of published commentary establishes a claim about one definition — say, that Denmark performs well — and applies it to another — say, that comprehensive state ownership works. Insisting on a stated definition before proceeding disposes of a surprising proportion of apparent disagreement.

The third is selective comparison. Comparing Cuba's health outcomes to the United States' while comparing its income to Switzerland's, or comparing Soviet growth to Britain's while ignoring the different starting points, produces whatever result the author wants. The methodologically defensible comparison is against countries with similar starting conditions in the same period: the USSR against Spain, Italy or Japan; Cuba against Costa Rica or the Dominican Republic; East Germany against West Germany, which is the cleanest natural experiment available and which ended with East German productivity at roughly 30 to 40 per cent of the West's.

Several questions remain genuinely open and will not be resolved by argument alone. Whether comprehensive planning is now computationally feasible is empirically untested at scale. Whether worker-managed firms can be made to invest adequately, given that members' claims on assets do not survive their leaving, has plausible solutions on paper and limited evidence in practice. Whether social democracy can be sustained under high capital mobility, or whether it requires international coordination that has proved elusive, is being tested in real time. Whether decarbonisation is compatible with growth is contested inside the tradition as much as outside it. And whether the enormous productivity gains from automation will be distributed as leisure, as unemployment or as rents to asset owners is the version of the question that will most likely dominate the next several decades.

The practical advice for a reader is unglamorous but effective: ask what specific institutional arrangement is being proposed, which country and period is being cited as evidence, what the comparison case is, and what would count as the proposal failing. Positions that cannot answer those four questions, from any direction, are not worth much.

guides.title: Liberalism
guides.summary: Liberalism is the political tradition built on individual liberty, rights, limited government, and equality before the law. This guide traces its origins, thinkers, principles, major branches, relationship to democracy and markets, its critics, and its condition today.

sections.heading: What Liberalism Is
sections.body: Liberalism is a political and moral philosophy built on the value of individual liberty. At its core stands a simple but far-reaching claim: that the freedom of the individual is a fundamental good, and that the central purpose of political institutions is to protect and enlarge that freedom rather than to override it in the name of tradition, religion, or collective glory. From this starting point flow the characteristic liberal commitments: to individual rights, to government limited by law and answerable to the governed, to equality before the law, to religious toleration, and to a private sphere into which public authority may not intrude without justification. The word itself entered political vocabulary only in the early nineteenth century, since the Spanish Liberales of 1810 were among the first to use it as a party label, but the ideas are older, and the tradition is usually traced to seventeenth- and eighteenth-century Europe. Because the label has been claimed by very different movements, it is important at the outset to separate several senses. In its broad, philosophical sense, liberalism is the family of doctrines centred on liberty, limited government, and rights, and in this sense most modern Western democracies, whether their governing parties call themselves conservative or progressive, operate within a liberal framework. In a narrower sense, liberal names a position on the political spectrum, and here usage diverges sharply: in the United States liberal has come to mean the centre-left, favouring an active welfare state and social reform, whereas in much of Europe liberal denotes support for free markets and is associated with the centre-right. A reader must always ask which sense is meant. Certain themes recur across all versions. Liberalism is individualist, treating the single person, rather than the tribe, class, or nation, as the basic unit of moral and political concern. It is universalist, holding that its principles apply to all human beings by virtue of their humanity, not only to members of a particular group. It is egalitarian, insisting that people share a fundamental moral equality even amid vast differences of talent and fortune. And it is meliorist, optimistic that societies and institutions can be reformed and improved by reason. Liberals disagree, often bitterly, about what liberty requires in practice, about how far the state should go to secure it, and about the balance between freedom and equality, but they share these organizing convictions. Liberalism is thus best understood not as a single fixed programme but as a broad tradition of argument, stretching from seventeenth-century struggles over religious toleration and royal power to present-day debates over markets, welfare, identity, and rights. The sections that follow trace its origins, its leading thinkers, its principles, and its major branches, before turning to the criticisms it has faced and its condition today.

sections.heading: Historical Origins
sections.body: Liberalism grew out of the upheavals of early modern Europe, and three great crises shaped it: the wars of religion, the struggle to limit royal power, and the intellectual revolution of the Enlightenment. Each pressed the questions that liberal ideas would answer. The Reformation of the sixteenth century shattered the religious unity of Western Christendom and plunged Europe into more than a century of savage confessional warfare, culminating in the Thirty Years War, which ended in 1648 and left much of Central Europe devastated. Out of this catastrophe came the first great liberal principle: religious toleration. If Catholics and Protestants could not agree on ultimate truth and could not exterminate one another, then perhaps the state should cease trying to enforce a single faith and instead permit believers to worship as their consciences dictated. The argument that matters of belief lie beyond the rightful reach of political power, most famously made in John Locke's Letter Concerning Toleration of 1689, became a template for the broader liberal idea of a protected private sphere. The second crisis was constitutional. In seventeenth-century England, kings claiming to rule by divine right clashed with Parliaments claiming ancient rights and control of taxation. The conflict produced civil war, the execution of Charles I in 1649, and finally the Glorious Revolution of 1688, in which Parliament deposed James II and installed William and Mary on conditions set out in the Bill of Rights of 1689. This settlement established that the monarch was subject to law and to Parliament, that political power was limited and conditional, and it furnished the practical model of constitutional, limited government that liberalism would theorize and export. The third source was the Enlightenment of the eighteenth century, an age that placed reason, science, and human progress at the centre of thought. Enlightenment thinkers subjected inherited authority, of church, crown, and custom, to rational criticism and asked what institutions free and reasonable people would choose for themselves. From the same current came the doctrine of natural rights: the idea that individuals possess rights simply as human beings, prior to and independent of any government, which government exists to protect. This idea received its most influential political expression in two revolutions. The American Declaration of Independence of 1776 proclaimed that all men are created equal and endowed with unalienable rights to life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness, and that governments derive their just powers from the consent of the governed. The French Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen of 1789 declared that men are born free and equal in rights. By the close of the eighteenth century, then, the raw materials of liberalism were assembled: toleration, limited and consensual government, natural rights, equality before the law, and faith in reasoned reform. The nineteenth century would organize them into a self-conscious political movement bearing the liberal name.

sections.heading: Key Thinkers
sections.body: Liberalism is the work of many hands, and a handful of thinkers gave its central ideas their classic form. John Locke, the Englishman whose Two Treatises of Government appeared in 1689, is often called the father of liberalism. Against the theory of the divine right of kings, he argued that legitimate government rests on the consent of the governed and exists to protect the natural rights of individuals to life, liberty, and property. In Locke's account, people in a pre-political state of nature possess these rights already; they form a government by agreement to secure them more reliably; and a government that systematically violates them forfeits its authority, so that the people may rightfully resist. This contractarian, rights-based reasoning became the backbone of liberal political theory and shaped the American founding directly. The Frenchman Montesquieu, in The Spirit of the Laws of 1748, contributed the doctrine of the separation of powers. Observing that concentrated authority tends toward tyranny, he argued that liberty is best preserved when the legislative, executive, and judicial functions are lodged in separate hands that check one another. This principle was written into the United States Constitution and became a cornerstone of liberal constitutional design. The Scottish philosopher Adam Smith, in The Wealth of Nations of 1776, supplied the economic dimension. He argued that when individuals are left free to pursue their own interests in competitive markets, the invisible hand of price and exchange tends to coordinate their efforts toward general prosperity more effectively than central direction can. Smith thus founded classical economic liberalism, though he was far from a doctrinaire advocate of unlimited markets, recognizing many proper tasks for the state. The German philosopher Immanuel Kant gave liberalism a deep moral foundation. His insistence that every rational being must be treated as an end in itself, never merely as a means, and his conception of persons as autonomous, self-legislating agents, grounded the liberal commitment to human dignity and individual autonomy in ethics rather than mere prudence. His essay Perpetual Peace of 1795 also anticipated liberal internationalism. The Englishman John Stuart Mill, writing in the nineteenth century, produced in On Liberty of 1859 the classic defence of individual freedom against social as well as governmental tyranny. His harm principle, that the only legitimate ground for coercing an individual is to prevent harm to others, remains the sharpest statement of the liberal limit on authority, and his advocacy of free speech and of the emancipation of women extended liberalism's reach. Later thinkers reshaped the tradition: T. H. Green and L. T. Hobhouse developed a more social liberalism around 1900, John Maynard Keynes reworked its economics, and John Rawls, in A Theory of Justice of 1971, revived liberal political philosophy for the modern age. Each built on the foundations these founders laid.

sections.heading: Core Principles
sections.body: Beneath liberalism's many variants lie a set of core principles that its adherents share, even as they dispute how to weigh and apply them. The first and most fundamental is individual liberty. Liberals hold that persons should be free to think, speak, worship, associate, work, and live as they choose, and that this freedom may be restricted only for compelling reasons, chief among them the protection of others' equal freedom. A classic distinction, sharpened by Isaiah Berlin in his 1958 lecture Two Concepts of Liberty, separates negative liberty, the absence of external interference or coercion, from positive liberty, the presence of the capacities and resources needed to act effectively. Classical liberals emphasize the former; social liberals stress that freedom is hollow without the latter. The second principle is individual rights. Liberals hold that individuals possess claims, to life, to liberty, to property, to expression, to due process, to conscience, that governments and majorities must respect and that are not simply theirs to grant or withdraw at pleasure. Whether these rights are grounded in nature, in reason, in contract, or in their good consequences is disputed, but the function is constant: rights fence off a protected sphere of the person against the power of the state and the pressure of the crowd. The third is limited government under the rule of law. Because power is dangerous, liberals insist that it be constrained: by written constitutions, by the separation of powers, by independent courts, and above all by the principle that officials as well as citizens are bound by known, general, prospective laws applied equally to all. The rule of law means that no one is above the law and that power is exercised through settled rules rather than arbitrary will. The fourth is equality, though liberals mean by it primarily moral and legal equality: the equal worth of every person and their equal standing before the law, with careers open to talent rather than fixed by birth. How far this formal equality must be supplemented by measures to reduce material inequality is one of the great internal debates of the tradition. The fifth is toleration and pluralism. Recognizing that reasonable people differ profoundly about religion, morality, and the good life, liberals hold that the state should not impose a single vision but should permit a diversity of beliefs and ways of living to coexist, intervening only to prevent harm. Underlying all of these is a distinctive stance: the government requires justification to the individual, and the burden of proof lies on those who would coerce, not on those who wish to be left free. Liberty is the default; restriction the exception that must be argued for. This presumption in favour of freedom, more than any single institution, is the thread that runs through the whole tradition.

sections.heading: Classical Liberalism
sections.body: Classical liberalism is the original form the tradition took in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, and it remains a living current of thought. Its distinguishing feature is a strong emphasis on individual freedom secured by strictly limited government, especially in economic life. The classical liberal ideal is the minimal or night-watchman state: a government confined to a few essential tasks, defending the country, keeping internal order, enforcing contracts, and protecting persons and property, and otherwise leaving individuals free to arrange their own affairs through voluntary exchange. Economically, classical liberalism champions free markets, private property, freedom of contract, and free trade. Drawing on Adam Smith, it holds that prosperity grows fastest when producers and consumers are left to make their own bargains, guided by prices, and that governments generally do more harm than good when they try to direct the economy, fix prices, or shield industries from competition. The nineteenth-century campaign against Britain's Corn Laws, protectionist tariffs on grain finally repealed in 1846, was a defining liberal victory, and free trade became a hallmark of the creed. The French phrase laissez-faire, meaning let it be done or leave it alone, captured the policy attitude, though few classical liberals took it to a pure extreme. Politically, classical liberals prize constitutional government, the rule of law, and the protection of civil liberties, and they are wary of concentrated power whether it is royal, aristocratic, or democratic. Many nineteenth-century liberals were in fact cautious about mass democracy, fearing that unpropertied majorities might vote to plunder minorities or trample individual rights, and they favoured limited franchises, checks on government, and protections for property. The tension between liberalism and democracy, explored later in this guide, was thus present from the start. The high tide of classical liberalism came in nineteenth-century Britain, whose Liberal Party under leaders such as William Gladstone stood for free trade, sound money, low taxes, limited government, and civil and religious liberty. Thinkers such as Herbert Spencer pushed the doctrine toward a thoroughgoing individualism, though this hardened into positions many later liberals rejected. In the twentieth century, as mainstream liberalism moved toward an active welfare state, classical liberalism was carried forward and revived by economists and philosophers who feared that the growth of government threatened freedom. Friedrich Hayek, in The Road to Serfdom of 1944, warned that central economic planning tended toward tyranny; Milton Friedman argued for markets and against state intervention; and Robert Nozick, in Anarchy, State, and Utopia of 1974, defended a minimal state on the basis of individual rights. This revived classical liberalism, often called libertarianism in its more radical American form, insists that economic freedom is inseparable from political freedom and that a large state, however well-intentioned, endangers both. It remains the chief rival, within the liberal family, of the social liberalism that came to dominate the twentieth-century mainstream.

sections.heading: The Liberal State and Constitutionalism
sections.body: Liberalism is not only a theory of the individual but a theory of the state, and its distinctive contribution to statecraft is constitutionalism: the idea that political power should be organized, limited, and made accountable by fundamental rules. A liberal state is one whose government is constrained by law, structured to prevent the concentration of power, and obliged to respect the rights of those it governs. The machinery that achieves this has several parts. The first is the constitution itself, whether written in a single document, as in the United States, or resting on statutes and conventions, as in the United Kingdom. A constitution establishes the offices of government, defines and limits their powers, and typically entrenches certain rights beyond the easy reach of ordinary legislation. Constitutionalism means that even the highest officials hold power under the constitution, not above it, and that changing the fundamental rules requires more than a momentary majority. The second is the separation of powers, Montesquieu's principle that the legislative power to make laws, the executive power to carry them out, and the judicial power to interpret and apply them should rest in different hands. Coupled with checks and balances, in which each branch is given some capacity to restrain the others, this arrangement is designed so that, in James Madison's phrase in the Federalist Papers of 1788, ambition is made to counteract ambition, and no single actor can seize unaccountable control. The third is an independent judiciary and the practice, in many liberal states, of judicial review, by which courts may strike down laws or acts that violate the constitution. The United States Supreme Court asserted this power in Marbury versus Madison in 1803, and many later constitutions granted it explicitly. Independent courts protect individual rights against transient majorities and hold officials to the law. The fourth is the entrenchment of rights, often in a bill of rights, which places certain freedoms, of speech, religion, assembly, and the person, beyond the ordinary give-and-take of politics. The United States Bill of Rights of 1791, the French Declaration of 1789, and the many national and international human-rights instruments of the twentieth century, such as the European Convention on Human Rights of 1950, all serve this liberal purpose. Underlying all these devices is the rule of law: the insistence that government act through general, public, stable rules applied equally, rather than through arbitrary command, and that officials be answerable in independent courts for exceeding their authority. The liberal state also rests on the consent of the governed, expressed through representative institutions and periodic elections, and on the freedoms, of press, association, and speech, that make genuine accountability possible. Constitutionalism is thus liberalism's answer to the oldest problem of politics: how to create a government strong enough to protect its citizens yet constrained enough not to threaten them.

sections.heading: Economic Liberalism and Markets
sections.body: Economic liberalism is the application of liberal principles to the production and exchange of goods, and it holds that individuals should be free to own property, make contracts, choose their work, and trade with one another, with the state's economic role kept limited. Its intellectual founder is Adam Smith, whose Wealth of Nations of 1776 argued that a market economy, in which self-interested individuals buy and sell at freely formed prices, tends to coordinate the efforts of millions of strangers into a productive whole without any central direction. The metaphor of the invisible hand captures the claim that private pursuit of gain can yield public benefit, as competition drives producers to supply what others want at the lowest sustainable cost. The core institutions of economic liberalism are private property, which gives individuals secure control over resources and an incentive to use them well; freedom of contract, which lets people make binding agreements on their own terms; competitive markets, which set prices and allocate resources through supply and demand; and free trade, which extends these principles across borders on the argument, developed by David Ricardo through the theory of comparative advantage in 1817, that nations gain by specializing and exchanging even when one is more efficient at everything. Economic liberals generally favour low and predictable taxes, sound money, balanced public finances, and a light regulatory touch, trusting decentralized decisions over central planning. The case for markets rests on several claims: that they harness dispersed knowledge no planner could gather, a point pressed by Friedrich Hayek in his 1945 essay on the use of knowledge in society; that they align private incentives with productive effort; that they respect individual choice; and that, historically, market economies have generated unprecedented growth in wealth and living standards. Economic liberals also argue that economic freedom and political freedom reinforce each other, since a state that controls all economic life controls the means of independence. Yet economic liberalism has always contained internal disagreement about the proper limits of the market. Even Smith recognized public goods, such as defence, justice, and certain infrastructure and education, that markets underprovide, and he was sharply critical of merchants' conspiracies against the public. Later economists identified market failures, including monopoly, externalities such as pollution, information asymmetries, and the instability of the business cycle, that provide liberal arguments for regulation, antitrust enforcement, environmental rules, and macroeconomic management. This is the fault line between two liberalisms: classical and libertarian liberals hold that markets, left largely alone, tend to correct themselves and that state intervention usually backfires, while social liberals hold that active government is needed to remedy market failures, cushion insecurity, and secure for everyone the material conditions of real freedom.
